On each pillow a curly head. Were they sleeping? they thought, not quite, • They had left the light that they aright Might Santa Claus see when he came at night, And, lo ! he was there in the great arm-chair And all around him the Christmas gifts were. "A bicycle new, that is for you," Said Ally to Philip, who took the same view, And on it he got and away was whirled, And faster and faster the great wheels twirled, And, alas! poor Philip head foremost was hurled, And didn't know where he was in the world. Then Ally-took up a great doll, and she Waa whisked away as quick as might ho Into a garden, and then she did see The queerest men and the queerest boys, And a large assortment of Christmas toys, And an owl that kept up a screeching noise. She felt rather shy, and inclined to cry, But a Man with a long nose said, "Oh, fie I- Why cry when there is no reason why? . • This is Santa Claus' garden, and he's close by This is Christmas Eve, and the funniest things , Happen to those to whom Santa Claus brings , Toys and joys, both to girls and boys, And sugar candy, too much of which cloys. And Santa Clans he thus said to me, *Punchinello, just let her see My fur-lined sledge, and my reindeer too, That over the snow so swiftly flew, • From the great pine forests, from far, from far, All by the light of the Polar star, To the Christmas garden in which you are.' " * The sun rose up4n the morning bright. "Ally," said Phil," / saw him last night," And Ally answered, "I was in a fright In the Christmas garden, with snow all white; I saw his sledge, and the swift reindeer • That brought the good old Santa Claus here." "Winter Blossoms," Little Folks' Annital for 1886.

j Itobert Ilelsby, M.D. That is my name, !I buve written it for a good many years now, but at 'the rim. the incidents occurred, which I am about to relate, and of which every succeeding Christmas time has brought me a happy reminder, I was a rather juvenile MD., with an insufficient practice to life. p me busy and prevent my indulging in hobbies in an amateurish way. ~ • . .

•, Among other things I dipped into phonograplty, learned the deaf and dumb alphabet, and iabbied in telegraphing, nnt With any thought of becoming an operator, or reporkee, or a teacher in 9 deaf wind dumb asylum, nor, in fact, with the thought of taming any ode of these acooniplishmente into Any mustiest use, but simply beeausel bad time on my -hands, and t these subjects had an interest and someVaing of fas- cination for me, enough cf, fascination ,certainly to lead, ixt devote ,to' them a good many' hours, Whicb, I dare say. might hate bee* much Plore wisely and priniently -given to study in my profession. , Roo-ever, 1 h&Y`e no reason to regret the time I gave to the alphaget&f telegraphytthat mystery of arbitrary F4OIIIIIIS nnli lines, long and short, by which words are ni,ell,ll and thought is conveyed to the initiated. I have nor only no reasorryt consider thisssone hobby of mine as a warrto of time, but I think you will agree with me beforeil shall have finished that it wae as good an 'in vetstinent of time as I could thave made. I awoke with a start on Christmas night 18 —, and sO-ang out of tied. Now, when I state' that the start arid spring were caused by the ringing of toy night. b4l. the old tpractioner, who is seasoned toi etch appeals, will smile a ready assent to .my avowal of juvenility and a limited practice, the seasoned physician waking up leisurely at the peal of his night bell, and rising with grumbling torpidity. - Bat this was the first time my own night-bell had cosi, rang, aced was down at the front door before the jingle had fairly ceased. As I threw the door open I saw a man on the step, and. a carriage drawn up to the °aria._ . .

." Is this Dr. Ilelsby t" The MLA before ms asked in a low wale, -bone. "Y(1," I asswered, -"car I be of any service 1" "I wish you would conic, with ine at once, if pos- sible. The case is urgent and, I fear, beyond remedy.' I went up stairs three steps at a time. My mother, who with say sister and myself formed our little household, had been loused, too, by the bell and was as the door a lher bedroom, looking a little scared.. "What is it, Bobert 1" she asked.

"A patient.] " • I exclaimed, crushing past her, " lyieg at the point of death." I h- ard what sounded like a timid prayer that it might not be a contagious sliseatte,•but I was already in my own !Doom dtetsaing reyself with a celerity I had never 'hewn eine+) my college days, when I dressed for morning prayers. I was soon in the carriage and on the way, but wit4lout the least idea as to where,' was going. My wind was altogether absorbed by wondering what my loatient was to be. "What is the trouble " I 45sked or the gentleman (att I took him to be) who had come for me. 4 'The debility•of old age, I fancy," was his answer still in that sense quiet, assured voice; "you will discover some odd things, no doubt. He was a man of eccentrio whims. We who have kiown him long are used :to his peculiarities but a stranger would be naturally surprised at irst. I thought it well to put you on your guard. it would be better not to shew before him any surprise at what you allay see."

I had a very strenuous desire to ask how it happened tha I should have been sent for, but my pride re- strained me. It seemed to me that I should have been betraying the surprise of a patientlese doctor if I allowed myself to ask that question, so I stiffed my curiosity as well as possible, and for the greater part of the way we rode in eilenoss while I was writing imeeinary prescriptions of mildly stimulazing nature, intended to arrest the natural decay of bodily F.n. eve. • . .

The carriage' stopped hrfie-e a detached ivonse stending in an ample gliFdeu and dowed by large tiers from what little light there was on this tia,on- less night. There was not a light anyerhere to be seen about the place, and the whole eiroct was very gloomy and dismal. Sombre! enough to kill aupane, young or old, I said to myself, ea I followed my con- docwir from the gate up the gravel walk. I Eallek get ar. pi4ieet out of this to begin with. mr guide gave a gentle tap with th 4 knocker, and the (tour was opened at once by a withered, bent old who bad been evidently waiting MOSY b 3-, so -arianpt had beeu the answer to the summons. We enteeed a direly-lighted hail, the only words spoken being .a roqueet from my guide that I woald follow him. Thu door was cloi-ed behind us by the old woman.; and we passed on to the rear of the broad entrance hall, in which raw no staircase to the upper rooms somewhat to my sur- prise. My guide turned the handle of a door and we stood presently In • little room. He offered me a chair and then, stepping to the side of the room, tonehed what looked to me like the button of an electric hell, close beside the only other door in the room than that by which we had entered. He remained standing in a listening attitude a few minute., then opened this second ddor and asked me to ember.. I stepped into what appeared to be a tiny lift, large enough for three or four persons; my guide entered after me, closed the door, pulled a cord, arid we began to slowly rise. All this had been done in such perfect silence, in such dim aud ghoetly light, and, withal, resented sech an extraordinary arrangement ef a private house, that I was uneomfortably affected by a cease of mystery, and was half inclined to wish I had been left undisturbed in my bed. It must he the owner of this dwelling, whom I have been called to see, I con- cluded, and this unusual way of reaching the upper floor of his house must be one of those eocentricities •of which my guide spoke in the carriage. I could not judge how many feet we had risen, when the lift stopped before another door. it was •opened, and we stepped out into another small room, much like that from which we had entered the lift below. I was desired to sit down and wait a moment, and my conductor left me. There was one window in this little room, but it was closed with heavy shutters, and these were barred. There was nothing else to arrest my attention, but I had not long to wait thus alone with my rather dis- turbed/directions. My conductor returned, asked ma to follow him, and led the way out into and aeross a broad corridor, which could not be called a landing, for there was no stairway visible here either. I was ushered into a large bedroom ; my guide followed me and closed the door, saying, "your patient, Dr. Heleby." It was a relief, to be assured that there was in truth a legitimate purpose in this night summons and I stepped qtiickly up to the bed, my roused professional interest predominating over all other sensations for the moment. I noticed for the first time as I neared the bed a female figure sitting in the shadow of the bed eurtains on the further side. My guide placed a chair for me, and then stationed himself at the foot of the bed. Both the man and the woman kept their positions throughout the interview, or, at least, while I remained near the sick man, and they watched very narrowly, all that occurred. And now as te my patient. He was an old man certainly, but it would have been difficult to guess his age with any assurance of accuracy. The gray locks were bag mad scattered ; the cheeks hollow and gaunt ; the lips pallid ; the eyes large and staring but with the light of intelligence, tkough life, it was plain to see, flickered dimly. His gaze, as it fell on my face, seemed to zee strangily eager and scrutiniz- ing. The figure, clearly lined beneath the light bed- clothes, was tall. Altogether he impressed me as a men who would have been in health of marlied strength of character and power-of will as well as strong and rugged in body. A few moments' observation inclined me to favour the suggestion my conductor had made in the carriage, that this was a case of the decay of the vital powers from old age. I discovered no symptoms of localised, disease. However, tasked him, "What seems to be the trouble f "

"Worn out," was his answer, in a faint whisper. I made no reply_ but placed. my fingers on his wrist to get the action of the pulse. The idttant I did 80, is fingers closed over towards my hand, instead of zemaining relaxed and quiescent, as is usually the .eise.. I was surprised at this. but much more sur- prised he moment after to feel the tips of his fingers gently pressing the back of my limit], where they touched. I moved my hand and he moved his, so as to still touch me with the finger tips, and renewed those singular pressures./ I say "singular," because it was not only a peculiar thing to do under the circumstances. but, I presently noticed that these pressures were uneven in length and forte. I cannot describe them bettor than as an irregular, fluttering beat upon my hand. 'I attributed it to nervousness; then I began tq think that I might have been mistaken in my first judgLaent us to bus sanity, but suddenly, 112 the midst of my perplexity, I was stirred by a vague bUt extraordinary sensation. It was as though some intelligence unseen by me was striving to communicate with me. I was under the spell of it. I straggled to understand it, to catch the

accents, as one night strain the sense of hearing to a voice calling from far away. Theo like a flash I seemed t 2 see a word as clearly as_t%ttglr printed in large type upon a white page, and that word was

"LISTEN."

I understood it I The man, who lay dying before me, was trying to talk with me in secret by a system of telegraphic signals in the long and short pressures of his fingers on my hands 1 That wihi,ch I had taken for a nervous fluttering, wati a determined and intelli- gent action. His mind was speaking to mine through that silent medium of the touch 1
Expressed in the Morse alphabet those long and short beats or pressures made the following oombina- Lion •

Apparently an unintelligible series of dote and lines ; hut in reality as they lie Printed 'on this page, these dots and lines have a significance for the skilled eye. Translated literaley into long and short sounds, they become equally significiot to the skilled ear, or they may in a sequence of short and long pressures of the &were speak again to the sense of touch. Through the senseof touch then I realised at last that my patient wes saying to me—" Listen." I had sufficient presence of mind not to betray my eerprise•oe my agitation to those keen, ivatching eyes eround the, bed. I did not stop at that critical moment to search for an answer to any of the wonder- ing questiens that obtruded themselves on my cons eciousness. I kept my fingers firmly on the dying resan's pulse, and with a quick series of return pressures t•bitl to bine " Yes, I . My eyes were on his, and I-saw.' the sudden gleam that poneed over his face. " Can you tuiderstaed "he tel-graphed. " s," I answered ; " go On. What is it ?" s' Will you be tette to me ? " "Yen certainly. You may trust me." '" My will is hidden in the mattress of 'this lied. I met to you to bring it to light When I am dead." " Why not now ? ' " No. They would destroy It, or kill you before you coeld leave this house." 1 I 'effected an instant. That seemed to me impossi- ble!, but yet who knew where I bad come? Might it not lie an easy matter to dispose of me? The man, who bed brought me to this house, knew that I had made -no inquiries of him 'before I had left my own home. and could not, therefore!, have left a clue by which I might be traced. I determined to be prudent, and meanwhile find oat all I could. "Has there heen foul play with you 2" I asked. " No, no! I am dying from nature' causes. They hove no hand in it. They only want my property." "What is your name 1' "Joseph Markler." "Is there anything else!" "Nothing else, The will in the mattress is my last one. Save it. Now prescribe something for me and go away. But be tine I" I will be tree ; trust me." No one can realise how strange it was to be carrying on this secret interchange of messages in plain sight of those wateising eyes and yet as hidden from them as if they had been a thousand tnilee from us. But the man, my conductor, who was still leaning over the foot of the bed, was evidently growing restiele at the prolonged silence. "Well,' he said, a little sharply, " What is your verdict, doctor ? " "Wait F" I answered, and then I became the physician once more; questioned my patient and made a thorough examination, and it last I wits satisfied. "I shall prescribe nothing btiftonios," I said, as I rose from my chair at the bedside. "I should insist ut on a change of air if he was able to move, or to be moved with safety." I wrote a preeoription ; an envelope was placed in my hands, which I put unopened in my pocket. I turned to my conductor and said, "I believe that is all now. Shall I be required again t" "1 will let you know, Dr. lefeleby," he answered, and led the way out of the room. We returned to the lift and, as we descended, I determined to try an experi- ment. "You have not yet t,old me the name of my patient, sir," I said to hira. He was evidently satieffed that there was no neces- tsity for any concealment now, • for he answered, "Joseph Markler." "And may I ask your name r 4. Henry Markler.." 4'A son I presume then." I suggested. "No; a nephew," he answered, but with el frown that did not encourage me to continue ray inquiries. But I was resolved to know where the house was, and I tasked. No. 3, Fordyce-terrace," was the un- gracious answer, and I put no more questions. The carriage was waiting to take me home, and there I found the good, anxious mother sitting up for my return. To have told her all the incidents of my visit would have only distressed her, and I made my account therefore as brief and, commonplace as possible. Then to forestall any too searching questions, I made a diversion by pulling from my pocket the envelope, which had been handed me, and which, I supposed, eon tamed my fee. • "Bat here, mother," I exolained, "is the. assurance of the whole matter. 'The labourer is worthy of his hire,' bet in thin case they fixed the value themselves. Let us see what my labour is rated at," and I drew from the envelope to my astonishment:four five-pound notes. To- tell the honest truth it was my first fee, and the sight of it made me jubilant. I even forgot myself in my amazement and delight, and betrayed ' a secret, which until now I had guarded as I supposed , even from the jealous fond eyes of a mother. "I will ask Alice to-morrow "I exclaimed. The smile on my mother'sgoe, recalled me. "Now you know," I said with some chargrin. "I have known for a good while," she answered, still smiling. " How ' I murmured in my surprise. "A son oannot keep his love hid, from etemother's eyes." "Well, I am glad you do know," I said emphatically; "I wish you could tell me, too, what my chances are." She still smiled, and that was encouraging, but there' was less assurance for mo in her words, when she spoke, "It. is not easy to read a girl's heart," she said to me, "but I am sure Alice Ramsey does not dislike you. I should be more afraid of her sensitive pride than of her heart, Robert. I think you will find her poverty your greatest obstacle." 'But I should relieve her from all that." I urged. "With your first fee ? " she asked, with another smile, • "No—no, mother I Yoteknow I am not dependent on es2y profession. I had determined, though, to make my first fee before I asked her to marry me.' "Well, I wish you God speed, my son, for I think she is worthy of you, and I am sorry for her, because her life is a hard one. But still I say, you have most to fear from a sensitive shrinking from joining her poverty to the lot of another, however mach she might love him." Alice Rumsey was my sister's- music teacher and, young as she was, an accomplished pianiste neverthe- less. Her father might have had a great name as a musician but for his wild and irregular habits. As it was he lived up to the extent of such income as he could get; died a worn-out man at forty-five, leav- ing his widow and daughter penniless. The widow had soon followed him, and the daughter was left at twenty-two to earn her own living. This is all my mother had learned of Alice Rumsey's past, when some ladies who bad become interested in Alice, asked her to make trial of the orphan girl as a teacher for my sister, Cora. She had not only proved 1 her own ability beyond all question, but had gained my mother's fullest confidence and interest, and had won my love. It seemed to me that my mother's warning was based on rather fanciful grounds. If Alice Rtuesey loved me, why should she suffer the fact of her position, as a penniless girl earning her own living, to stand in the way of her happiness and mine? But I did not realise the strength and depth of that pride, which shrinks not alone from the ungenerous con- struction of others, brut from a personal sense of incurring an unrequited obligation. Why could she not see. as I so clearly did, that what I gave was as nothing in comparison with what I asked in return and what she could give. That was the burden of my perplexed questioning and sorely disappointed heart, when I came from Alice Rumsey the next day, a rejected lover. I had gone to her in hope; I came away in despair, for in spite of her gentleness, in spite of the pain it caused her, alt it seemed to me, to refuse me, still she had re- fused me, and in such a way, too, as convinced me that her decision was an irrevocable one; I could not hope to change it. , And my wooing had been worse than useless, for it had made it impossible that she should continue coming to our house to give my sisters le.seons. She herself wrote to my mother begging to be allowed a release from her engagement.- It is not my purpose bt dwell on my own dis- appointment, ouly to teeoe as briefly as I can on each link of the strange chain of events which boand my life to the life of "the sweetest woman that e'er drew ' breath." On the day following my offer-and its rejection, I was called upon to maee a certificate of the causes of ' death of one Joseph Markier, who had died the night 'before at NO. 3, len clyee-terrace. I made the oertie- rate, and then, ietiorept of the steps I ought to take, I laid before my bolicitor the whole story of my I adventure two nights before. It is unnecessary tI detail the steps by which we compelled the dis- coverY of a Lalf-s4e4lt of notepaper, secreted ire

the mattress of the bed on which Joseph ?dart died. He had torn a tiny hole in the cover, had rol the paper into as small a compass as he could a thrust it there to stay till he was dead. Probably I was the only person he seen or been permitted to see, to whou.,' her could confide that secret; and he had, been able to entrust it with safety to mo. only because we both knew the Morse alphabet. It will never be known, although I have often tried to pio- ture, how be succeeded in eluding the vigßantr watch- fulness of those who were about him. They trusted, of course, to the impossibility of his executing an in- strument of sufficient formality to hold good in ar as a testamentary disposition of his property without their knowledge, and it was curious to note by wrist devices he had obtained witnesses to his signature. One was a locksmith, who had bees employed for a half-hour to repair the lock on the door of the bed- room, another was the old crone who bad admitted me to the house, and the third—strangest of all—' chimney sweep. But I have yet to disclose the most marvellous link, of all this chain. When that tiny,scrap of paper wee found and opened, it read as follows "I, Joseph Markler. hereby devise and bequeath to my only grandchild, Alice Rummy, daughter of Carl and Mary Ramsey, all my property, real and personal, of every description whatsoever, and I r evoke all other wills by me made." I omit the date and the signatures; but it will be easy to conceive my emotions when I read that docu- ment Was this--could, this be the Alice Rnmsey whom. I loved ?- It took ro long .me to prove that fact, however. My Alice was in truth the granddaughter of my first patient, of old Joseph Markler. The stern old roan ,- incensed at his daughter's marriage with Carl Rumsey against his will, had disowned her and hers, and bad persisted in that disownment until near his death. He had even purposed ignoring his granddaughter as well after as before his death,and had, left the great bulk of his property by a will 'executed some years before to his nephew, the Henry Markler whom I had met; but for- giveness and a kindlier spirit came at last, and he strove to remedy the cruel wrong he would have once committed. By how narrow a chance he had succeecied the reader knows. Of course there, was a furious contest made by the Marklers to prevent the probating of that scrap of paper as Joseph Markler's will, but they failed. My evidence was of the utmost importance, both as to the dying man's declaration that this was his will, and as to his soundness of mind. It was only after it was all over that Alice said to me one day, "What can I ever do, Dr. Helsby, to show my gratitude? " I held out both my hands in silence; she looked into my eyes with one timid, but happy glance, arid then she put her hands in mine, and I drew the dear head to my ehoulder with a new throb of tliankful- nen for my first patient.
[T3E END.]

ITtsell, SATURDAY NIGIIT,—M, Teanoff, Minister of the Interior, has eent the following reply to a Note addressed to the Bulgarian Government yeeterday by the representatives of Austell., Germany, Russia, and Italy:—" In view of the explaaations given by the ARKTiAR 'representative, accord- ing to which the Military Commission will take account of both vietories and defeats on either side, and will require the evacuation of Bulgarian territory by the Servians, and the continued occupation of hervian territory by the Bulgarians, until the clod usion of peace, as a guarantee for the corn- Pensation dee to Bulgaria, and in view also of *he telegram from the Turkish Grand Vizier announcing that the Com- mission would take into account 'the advantages acquired by the Bulgarians. the Government of Prince elexande• declares its readiness to submit to the deciaiees of tbe Commission." Liemenent-Colonel Cerruti, the Italian delegate, has Nen rh"- P-ssident of the Military Commission. •'a Servian troops are now in winter quarter,' and t•isS, , the rano:sets are expoeed. TIIE MILITARY COMMISSION. Niscn, Moene.Y.—The members of the Military Com- mission have viewed the Servian 'and Bulgarian positions near Pirot, accompanied by a Servian or Bulgarian repre- sentation, according to the side rhey were visiting, but neither the Bulearian nor the SErvian representative takes I part in the deliberaiione of the Commissioners or crosses the lines. Count Khevenhueller has arrived, and will .remain here until the Cernatiesion has pronounced its decision, CONSTANTINOPLE, .MONDAY,—Tile Military Commission at Pine having requested Servia and Bulgaria, as a pre- liminary ceudition, to declare that they will accept its de- cision, Prince Alexander has telegraphed to the Grand Vizier, asking whether the Sultan, as Sovereign, would ap- prove such acceptance on the Prince's part, and pointing] out that it would necessitate his eventually qui, tiug Pirot without a guiraetee for the future, or any indemnity for the Bulgarian victories. AN ARMISTICE YROTOCAL SIGNED. BELGRADE, Tmesnev.—An official Announcement is made here to-day of the signature. yeeterday evening of the prec- tocol of an armistice until March 1 between Sarvia and Bul- garia, based upon the conditions fixed by the Military Commission. The Servian and Bulgarian delegates also appended their signatures. The fulfilment of the conditions is to commence on the Servian side by the evacuation of the Bulgarian territory in Servian occupation. A. neutral zone of three kilometres will be established on either side of the Servo-Bulgarian frontier. Servian and Bulgarian delegates charged to negotiate for the conclusion of peace are to be immediately appointed. BELGRADE, WEDNESDAY.—A collision it reported to have occurred yesterday at Yeleskitza between some Bulgarian volunteers, who are charged with being the aggressors, and two companies of Servian troops. Several of the Bulger- lens were taken prisoners. FRANCE. THE ELECTION TO THE PRESIDENCY. PARIS, SATURDAY.—The Chamber of Deputies to-day, by 293 votes to 212, invalidated the election for the depatt- ment ol Landes. H. Goblet, Minister of Public Instruction, said the Government intended to fix an early date for the elections. The Minister concluded by stating that the Cabinet had decided upon convoking the Congress for the 25th inst. Baron Mackau insisted that there was a connec- tion between the date for the meeting of the Congress and that of the by-elections, and declared that the election of a President by an incomplete Congress was a serious emotion. The subject then dropped, and the House ad- journed. THE FRANCO-CHINESE. WAR. Pants, &emu:ram—A Yellow-book dealing with Chinese affairs Las been distributed to the Chambers to-day. A de- spatch of M. de St. Chaffray, President of the French De- limitation Commission in Tonquin, reports that the Com- mission started on the 10th inst., and expected to reach Langson on the 20th Inst. M. Cogordan, in a despatch from Shanghai of the 12th inst., announces that he saw Lisilung-Chaog the previous day, and then opened nego- tiations for a France-Chinese commercial treaty. Li-Hung- Chang was to communicate shortly a detailed Note stating the views of the Chinese Government and ite counter pro- posals in record to the draft submitted by France. THE MURDERS IN BURM Ali. The political agent at Manipur has received a letter frem Morgan stating that himself, Brette, the two Bnckstulls, Hill, Ross, and Baker are well and safe, but that Allen, Mencure, and Roberts had been murdered. THE GREAT SOCIALIST TRIa L AT WARSAW. WARSAW, MONDAY.— Judgment has been delivered in the trial which has been proceeding here eince the 27th ult. of the persons accused of belonging to the social revolutionary association styline itself "The Pro- letariate." Berdoweky, a juttice of the peace; Lure, a cap- tain of Engineers, and four other of the prisoners were sen- tenced to be hanged; eighteen were condemned to sixteen years' hard tabour in the mines, two to ter years and eight months' penal servitude with exitelor life to Siberia, and two 'others to transportation to Siberia for life. te ‘ TURKISH PREPARATIONS FOR WAR WITH sa. • GREECE. SMYRNA. MONDAY.—Of 60,000 reserve men registered in this vilayet, 32,000 hane now been mobilised. The last batch of 3,090 [nen left to-day for Salonica. The transport of troops has been conducted thronehost in the most economical way. The cost of conveying offleers, men, and horses from here to Salonica, a. distance of 250 miles, nee amounted to one silver inedjidie each, luggage being taken free of charge. PARIS, Moesnaen—According te authentic ad vices received here, the military precautions taken by Tarkey on the Hal- lenic frontiers leave little hope Df Greece being able to take up arms with any probability of Success. It is estimated that not fewer than 80,000 Turkish trope have passed through Salouica within toe past few days en their way to the Epirus. Altogether, the Porte has about 200,000 sole dierei concentrated in Macedonia, Albania, and other points threatened. On the other ground, Greece is not idle, and in spite of these formidable forces, continues her preparations for war. At present she is said to have more than 50,000 ' troops massed on the frontier, and expects to be able to bring the number up tecloo,ooo. FUNERAL OF KING FERDINAND OF ! PORTUGAL. Lesnoet, MONDAY.—The funeral of the bee King Ferdi- nand took place to-day. Tha ceremony, which was cons ] ducted in strict accordance with the offichl programme, was witnessed by a large crowd, who appeared to sympathise 'warmly with the Royal fancily. The coffin which was covered With wreathe of natural flowers, wasfollowed to the grave by the English, Russian, Spanish, Belgian, Italian, 1 and Brazilian Ministers, who represented their respective Sovereigns. The religious eervice in the Church of the Pantheon was also attended by Vice-Admiral Fellowes, in Command of the Channel Smadron, which is at present in the Tagus. All the places ot business were closed to-day 1)n account of the funeral. LEOPOLD VON RANKE'S NINETIETH BIRTHDAY. BEetatte, MoenAv.—The 90th birthday of Prof. Leopold von Ranks, the eminent historian, was celebrated here to-day at the nonagenarian's residence,where there was a laree at- tendance of distinguished personaves, the Crown Prince being among those who came to offer their congratulations in parson. The Emperor sent an autograph letter, couched in gracious termis,eecompanied by his portrait, and the Em- press also forwarded le congratulatory letter through Gen. Stranhberg. The Ministete congratulated the aged historian in a collective latter signed by all the members of the Cabl- net. Professor Auwers delivered an address on behalf of the Berlin Acedernv, and Rector Ileinert ono from the Univer- sity, a bile Of the provincial un versit les, Strassburg, Lein- Bic, and Jeua sent congratnlitiois by the hands' of Proles- sere Weissaecker, Maerenbrecher, and Lorerz. Herr von .Forchenbeck attended on behalf oethe Berlin Municipality. After r2ceiving the felicitations ot the assembled company PrOfeSSAr Ranks made a speech of rnme length, expressing warm acknnwiedgments of the numerses marks of honour extended to him. MADRID, IUESDAY.—The impaecia/ teeday states that 3 Republican conspiracy of an important cbaractrr has been discovered it Tarragona, but publishes no deteils of the affair.

*TUE UNITED STATES. NEW YORE, TEESUAY.---rhe attempt to rescue the miners imprisoned in the colliery at Nanticoake, Pennsylvania, has been anandoned owing to the further subsidence of earth, which realm the work cf excavation hopeless. It is not

• expected that the bodies of the victims will be recovered for a fortnight. Congress has Adjourned for the Christmas recess until January 5. The exports of produce from the United States for the past week amounted in value to 86,444,000. FRANCE AND MADAGASCAR. COMPLETE SURRENDER OF THE HOVAS. PAD'S, TUESDAY, 3-50 ?X. —The French Govornment has received a telegram from Madagascar announcing the concluAon of. a treaty of peace with the Roves. LAyErt.—lt is reported that the treaty gives France a protectorate over the whole of Madagascar. There will be a French Resident at Anrananarlyo charged with the con- duct of foreign affairs, and attended by a permanent guard. I The French wcupy Tainatave until the payment of an in- demnity of 10 million francs. M. de Freycinet, daring the sitting of the Chamber to- day, confirmed the news that peace had been s'gned between France and Madagascar. The Minister then explained that under the treaty just concluded the French Resident at An- tananarivo would be the indiSporiSable medium of communi- cation between the Queen and Foreign Powers, and all Her Majesty's diplomatic correspondence would pass through his bands. Frenchmen would be permitted to effect and renew leases for indefinite terms. France reserves to her- self he right to occupy the Bay of Diego Juarez, and there to construct all such works or buildings as she might deem expedrent. The Bovas would pay an indemnity of ten millions francs to compensate Frenchmen and other foreirners for any damage they might have sustained. The ',retch would continue to hold the port sad Custom-house of 'Tamatave until the indemnity was pail. Both France and the Queen of the lievas equally undetook to treat with humanity the native allies on either sidt. The state of affiirs in the north-eastern part of the island would be male the subject of special conventions.

div.head: THRILLING ADYENTUU ON LAKE
div.p: A THRILLING ADYENTUU ON LAKE

ST. CLAIR. DETPOIT, MICH., Dec. 9.—Three fishermen, living tic Grosse Puiat, 14 miles above this city, on Leise St. jlair, bad a thrilling experience yesterday Ad the sight befere. Their names are John Veraier, Charles ileum and Victor Bosseau. They left tlseir homes on Monday afternoon in a fishing boat, goieg out into Lake St. Clair to take up theis ground •iets for the winter. They were caught by the cold snap of Mon- day and frozen in. The ice was tee heave for them to row through, and not strong enough fix them to walk on. As a result they were corapellet to stay out all night in the piercing crld, with nothisg to eat or drink, and with no covering or other skeane of keeping warm. When day broke yesterday two of them could be seen in the boat standing ip and breaking the ice with their oars, and at tiinei stop- ping to warm themselves by slapping their Lards on their shoulders. One of the men occasionala ven- tured out on the ice with the painter of the beat in his band to try and drag her along. At last he was seen to break through the i.e and pull himself back by the rope. The third man could be observed by ° the aid of glasses from the steeple of an old French church, lying in the bottom of the boat, appal-fitly helpless. A blinding snowstorm Feet in at this tine, and a fierce wind sprang up, piling the ice in high banks along the shore, and the situation becane every moment more critioal..A desperateelfort to rescue the imperilled men was resolved upon, their distracted relatives making frantic appeals to the aasembled crowd of people to do this. A large fishboat wasscoured, full;• epuipped with pike poles, life lines, and grapplini hooks, and a stock of provisions. shortly,after eight o'clock the boat was pushed out into the grinding ice, manned by six men. The crowd en shore watched' the rescuers until a veil of snow intervened. The men in the boat were last seen working with a will and urging their craft slowly but surely in the direction of the enterers. Theee was a long and perilous trip before them. They were obliged to go at least a mile and a half out into the lake before being anywhere near the imperilled men. Then a groping search through the snowstorm was probable. Finally there was to be the struggle back to shore. As the day wore along the anxious friends on Above began to realise the peril to which the rescuing party had ex- posed themselves. It began to be feared that nine men instead of three would be lost in the blinding storm, and it was determined to secure •a tag-at Detroit and send her in search of the two parties. During the day two parties came to this city to secure help. Late in the afternoon a ferryboat left her route in the river and steamed up into Lake St. Clair, in the direction where the men were supposed to be. In the meantime efforts did not,slacken in the immediate vicinity. In the afternoon the storm abated, so that both of the parties in the ice could be seen !rem shore. About two hundred excited people lined the banks and watched each foot of headway which the rescue party made. The boat moved very slowly, however, and it became apparent that the relief would be too late. Then Richard Moran and his two sons determined to adopt a new -course. Instead of tailing a large and cumbersome fishboat they rigged several light duck skiffs with rollers underneath. These could be rapidly propelled through the water and rol- led over the ice. The trio started out, and were soon , abreast of the first rescue party. The latter had abandoned their efforts and turned back to the shore. The Morena reached the sufferers about four o'clock, and the crowds alone- the bank were crazy with joy , and excitement at the successful result. Then the homeward trip was cemmenced. It was observed on shore that but five figures worked with the:pike poles. At five o'elock a shout went up as the frail skiffs pushed over the shore ice, and the three brave rescuers and two survivors stepped ashore. The joy soon turned to sorrow, as it. was learned that young Chr.rlie Reno was at the bottom of the lake. The two survivors were more dead than alive, but in disconnected words they told how young Reno had heroically struggled to save them all, and finally died in the attempt. The party had despaired of get- ting assistance from land. Their only safety seemed to be to walk over the floating ice. Whether it would sustain them was a doubtful question, but Reno finally determined to solve it. He stepped out on a broad cake, and was seen flying landward over crunching ice and intervening stretches of water. Suddenly he disappeared. Theavater closed over him, and then the ice. The sufferers were horrified to see their companion die before their eyes, without any possible effort on their part to save him. They suf- fered intensely from hunger. Their sturdy frames withstood the cold, but broke down from want of food. There is little chance of securing Reno's body before next spring. The deceased was a well known young French resident of the Point, and a descendant of one of the early settlers. He was about 28 years old and unmarried.—Nese York Timm

Antony Ashley Cowper, Earl of Shaftesbury, of 24, Grosvenoraquare, was proved in Lon- don on the 11th inst., under the value of £28,000 person- alty. He devises all his real roperrv, including estates in Hampshire, Wiltshire, and Donetshire, to his eldest son, the present earl, in fee. The whele of his personalty he be- queaths among his children. I THREATENING THE PRINCE OF WAT,ES.—The further examination of John and Mary France Magee, on a charge of attempting to extort money from the Prince of Wales took place on Wednesday at Boy-street Police Court. No evidence was offered against the weinan. and she was dis- charged. Evidence was gives by the Secretary to the Prince of Wales of the reception of the threatening letters at Sandringham, and those documents were read to the Court by Mr. Poland, who appened for the prosecution. The male prisoner was committed for trial. TuE NETHEI2BY HALL OCTRAIE.—A man named Baker, who is said to have taken part in the recent outray,es in Cumberland, was arr(sterl in London on Wedneeday. Three men, one of whom is also named Baker, have already been committed for trial on charges of burglary at Netherby Hall, attempting to murder two police officers, and murder- ing a third constable. Baker is belteved to have been the fourth man seen in their company. Ile was taken to Car- lisle on Wednesday, hut so far be does not appear to have been conclusively iclantitied„ HEARTLESS CASE OF ELopparszer.—On Tuesday evening a case which excited 50035 interest was decided at Neston, Cheshire. John Go)ding, a young man, was charged with • stealing wearing aptarel from William Goodwin, and Jane Goodwin, wife of tho prosecutor, who appeared in the dock alongside, was also ::harged with taking her husband's pro- perty. The elopement was one of peculiar heartlessness and cruelty. The prosecutor is a enflamed invalid from rheu- matism. The male prisoner was a lodger. On the 7th inst. ; he and Mrs. Goodwin eloped together, taking with them 'A considerable proper- belonging to ir. Goodwin. They , were traced to Leiceqer. where they were apprehended with the stolen property is their possession. Mrs. Goodwin said that her husband thPatened to take her life when he was able to leave his bed, and she ran away. The magistrates characterising it as aheitrtless and 'cruel case, sentenced the ; prisoners each to twomontbs' hard labour.

div.p: • WAIIIINGTON SCFIOOL OF ART. ANNUAL REETING- AND PRIZE DISTRIBUTION. The annualmeeting of the eubeeribers to the above schoo was held at the schools on Friday night last week. The chair was taker by Mr. John ltylands. Letters of apology for non-attendaace were read horn Mr. P. Stable, Mr. J. C. Parr, and Mr. dimes Masson. VASTER'S REPORT. The report °Wm iIEAD MASTER (Mr. Berko) was read, as follows :—ln presenting to you my report for the last session, I beg to Brent your attention to the act that this institution has again maintained the high position that it has hitherto held. The school year extended from the lich of August, 1884. b the beginning of July, nos. and was attended by 221 sbdents, showing an increase in the num- ber attending the dasses of 49 during the year. This num- ber includee the numbers in the science classes. In April 3;000 drawings wire submitted to the examiners at Senth Kensington to compete for marks, certificates, and prizes. In May You conducted the science and art examinations in this building, with the following results; Eighty-seven second grade papers weresuccessfutly worked, whilst out of the number 14 were marked " excellent," which entitle the stu- dents to a pries. In science subject I (practical plane geometry), three students passed first-class elementary, and two etudents passed second-class elementary do. In baild- iug constriction (science subject DJ), four students passed firet•class elementary, and one student passed aecond-classdo. Ten students submitted 25 drawings for the art class teachers' and the third grade certcates. Of these 15 ware accepted, and at the personal examination held in May the same students passed successfully in twelve subjects. The prize list will show that sixteen second grade prizes and nine third grade prizes have been gained by the students of this school. You have supplemented the above list, with a local prize list, and the prizes yen have awar- ded to those students, who, although not obtaining government awards, have neverthelees executed meriterewe work during the year. For higher successes achieved by the students I would mention the bronze medal (national Competition prize) gained by Mr. Rollins Allen, the four second grade and two science subjects passed successfully. by Mr. J. ,Cameron, and the art class teachers' certificate by Miss Annie Chrimes, completed in one year. Consider- ing our improved accommodation and longer unrelaxed hours of study we anticipated increased successes, but the above figures have qui,J met our anticipations. By your kindly granting the request of the students to establish a vacation sketching club in connection with this school, and end also by your encouraging the students in this work you have matet Lilly assisted in the advancement of an important branch of study carried on in this Institution. In conclueion, I would express to you my appreciation of ,the valuable services rendered to me during the past session by my ass sistant master, Mr. C. B Aylward, and would also tender my thanks to Mien M. Burgess, Messrs. G. Ormancla, and Hollinn Allen for their ready assistance, ' SECRETAIIT'S REPORT. The Bow. SEC. (Mr. W. Owen) read his report as folk lows :—This, our second session in the new school build- ing, has proved to be as successful as we could have hoped both in the increased number of students taught and in the, result of their work, but owing to the additional expenses. we have incurred in obtaining a staff sufficient for con- tinual tuition daring school hours, which we hays increased from 17 hours per week to about 115• hours per week, our financial statement is not so good as the committee could wish. The session commenced with a fund in hand of £24 lie and closed with an adverse balance of 1,35 2s this however, the fees of the present session have already covered and your committee hope by an increased number of etudente' fees and a larger list of subscribers to weather the current session more prosperously, foeling.that the suc- cess of the lengthened hours of tuition and general working of the school is worth a special effort to centinue. The list of annual subecribers has more than doubled, having risen from £l7 lie to £4l, and in addition to these sntactiptions we have to gratefully acknowledge the receipt of £22 7s 2d from the committee of the Science School, lately held at Arpley Station, being the balance. after winding tap all their accounts. Your committee would urge the claim of ..he school upon those not already assisting us with annual bbscriptions he a very proper object for their help and Trould appeal with confidence to the public for funds to rusiat us in so good a work. It is quite possible that our stncess will force upon us the consideration of further ex- tending the school buildings at some early date. On the motion of Mr. J. RYLANDS, seconded by Mr. R. Gait:Err, the aboye reports were adopted. ELECTIONS. It was resolved, on the motion of Mr. F. MoNto, see in- ded iy Mr. J. E. secretars. . PRIZE DISTRIBUTION. The prizes were afterwards distributed to the successful students by Mr. W. Beamont, Mr. J. THE HOME RULE QUESTION. MR. GLADSTONE AND LORD HARTINGTON.

The following statement waa telegraphed on Saturday te ' London trom Hawarden "&f Mr. Crledetone should at any time have any plan or , intention to announce on the question of Irish Government it will be done publicly on his own responsibility, sad not by anonymous and irreeponeible declaration. Political , friends are assured that be remembers his obligations to them, and may safely understand that be is bound to none of the ideas announced, in his name. After saying this, Mr. Gledstose will hold himself excused from replying, in the present state of facts, to any further loeletriee, rumours. o- suggestions." The following letter has been addressed by the Marquis of Hertington to Mr. Thomas Brooks, chairman of his Lord- ship's nlention Committee in liossendsle "Devonshire House, Piccadilly, W., 19th December. ' "Dear Mr. Brook,'—My name has recently been he- ' quota!, mentioned in connection with reports on the sub- ject of a scheme of Irish policy which is stated to have been under the consideration of the leaders of-the Liberal party. I shall not within the next few weeks have an op- , portanity of adireseing rny constituents in public, sad I I think that the respect which I owe them justifies me in writing to you, as the chairman of my Election Committee, for the purpose of giving the most emphatic contradiction to all such reports so far se they relate to my- self. No proposals on the policy to be adop- ted by the Liberal party in reference to the demand of a large number of Irish members for the legislative independence of Ireland ties been communicated to me, and I see no reason to depart in any degree from the declarations which I have made er the opinions which I , have expressed is my speeches during the late election in Laneashire or elsewhere on the policy AnnoUnced by Mr. Parnell as the leader of the Irish Parliamentary party.—l remain, yours very truly, "EllatioNOTON." Although Mipisters think it their duty to meet the new Parliament without resigning office or proposing to resign, their present intention is not to proceed to any important befallen without receiving the sanction of the House of Commons for their maintenance in power. Their determi- nation (says the St. James's Gazette) is that it shall be well understood on all hands, before business begins, that they are not a Government "on sufference." ino Government can be effective which is exposed to the taunt of emitting at the pleasure of the Opposition, and Lord Salisbury's Ad- ministration will decline to go on unless it receives from the House of Commons a distinct and sufficient expression of desire that t should continue to conduct the affairs of the empire. Her Majerty's Government are prepared, we be- lieve, to enlarge local government in Ireland considerably. But under no circumstances will they either propoee or eauction any scheme for : setting up an Irish Parliament, under' any limitations or "guarantees whatever. Lord Derby, writing to the Central News; says the scheme of Home Role attributed to Mr. Gladatone has been mate- rially modified by subsequent statements from the right hen, gentleman disclaiming the plan alleged to have been put forward by him. Lord Derby therefore thinks it is ob- vious that it would net in any case be possible for him to expeesa his opinion of a scheme of which at the time of writing he had only seen a telegraphic summary. Mr. W. E. Forster, writing from Torquay under date De- cember 18, says that had he been well enough to see at the time the telegraphic summary of the scheme of Home Rule attributed to Mr. Gladstone he would have stated that he I was not prepared to give an minion upon such an unau- thorised eratemtrat of Mr. Gladstone's opinion. Mr. Forster adds that he does not think at present he would be inclined to express kis views on the Dish question. Speaking at Todmorden on Saturday evening, Mr. Brad. laugh said a change of leadership was of great importence for the Liberals. They could not expect Mr. Gladstone to eontiaue to lead them longer in his old age. It was said that the result of the elections had been to piece Mr. Par- nell in the nosition of leader, but this was not true. Ire- land had suffered much misery in the past, and he should vote for Home Rule. At a great Loyalist demonstration at Armagh, resolutions , were passed calling upon all Loyalists to unite and resiBt ' any attempt at giving Home Rule to Ireland, which eould only end in civil war; and also commending the cause of Loyalty in Ireland to the eympathetic support of the Prd- testants of England and Scotland.—Brother Foster, district master of the Orange Ledge of Dentgel, said they would tell their repreeentativee in Parliament that.if they precipi- tated the country into civil war immediately, they would be doing their duty if they could not prevent the separation from England in any other way.—Brother Peel, district master of Arrnagh, said that if civil war they must have,' they would have it, for the Orangemen of Ulster could bring an army of 60,000 men into the field if necessary. The London evening journal which originally "re- vealed " Mr. Gladstone's intentions with regard ti Ireland persists in the assertion that it knows more of the right hon. gentleman's mind than he does himself, and it more- over calmly assures Lord Hartington that be will have to " take his foot up again." The St. James's Gazette and the Globe concur in assuring us that Lord Salisbury intends to challenge a vote of confidence as soon as the Please of Com- mons is constituted. Mr. Trevelyan stated on Monday to a representative of a press agency that after Mr. Gladstone's communication and Lord HartiNgton's letter he felt satis- fied, so far as he (Mr. Trevelyan) was concerned, in letting the matter rest. He had the gravest anxieties with regard to the condition of Irelend, but the situation had been pro- duced very deliberately by the action of the Gove,nutent, and his intention was to wait until they had explained 'heir views before offering criticises and advice, which mieht be founded on imperfect and incorrect information. Mr. Storey, M.P., was also interviewed on Monday He stated that the Irish people having demanded in an unmistakable manner an Irish Parliament in Dublin, that demand must be conceded. Archbishop Croke, in a letter referring to some impertinent personalities in the Pall Mall Gazette, incidentally remarks that he "possibly may have declared himself against separation from England as being impracticable" and adds that "he is of the same mind as the Irish leaders on that point." Sneaking at a Meeting of Greenwich Conservatives on Monday night, Baron De Worms, Secretary to the Board of Trade, •sall the Government were prepared to adhere, in regard to their Irish Policy, to Lord Salisbury's declarations at Newport. They would begrudge to Ireland no measure demanded by jntice, bat the juetice which sedition-mongers were de- manding was not justice to Ireland and would be injustice tee:England. They were willing to extend to Ireland such measures of local self-government as were due, but there was a vent difference between that and a measure granting Home Rule, which meant, in plain English, separation from this country and Irish independence. The "Grand Orange Lodge of Ireland" met en Monday in Dublin and adopted an address to their brethren in Greet Britain and Ireland. The Orange leaders remark that never in the history of the Protestantism of this realm has the aspect of affaire been more threatening Hun it is now, and it is pointed out that a relaxation in any degree of the ties which connect Ireland with England will lead to ultimate separa- tion, to the ruin of the country an to the establishment et the most vulnerable points of the empire of a drill ground for hostile armies and a dockyard for foreign 'sets. An appeal is therefore made to those who realise the imminent peril which confronts them to stand shoulder to shoulder in defence of the Uaion. The address bears the signatures, "Erne, President," and "Eoniskillen, IOM." Lord B. Grosvenor agrees that the description of the var- ious stories about his recentsvisits to Chester and Dublin having an important political signifcance as "constructive fictions "is a perfectly accurate description. He declares that the report in the Dublin papere that he had an inter- view with Mr. Pernell at Chester is absolutely untrue, as the Irish leader was not within 200 miles of Cheater at the time Lord Richercl passed through that city. His lordship has been at the trouble to give to a new agency represen- tative a minute account of his movements during the past few days, and has gone so far as to explain his smallest actions while at Hawarden, Chester, Dublin, and other places—even to the cleaning of his guns for shooting, and preparing for dinner. Lord R. Grosvenor closed his inter- view with the reporter in a very amusing way by remark. ing that "he had nothing to say upon the Home Rule question, and that Mr. Gladstone was in excellent health and spirits." Mr. Parnell was again approached on Tuesday by an in- dustrious interviewer, but the hon. gentleman was " diem- dined ts formulate his demands." Mr. Parnell, we are told, has " again left London, but is within easy reach of the metropolis." Failing with Mr. Parnell, the reporter waited upon Mr .1. O'Kelly, M.P., who met his interrogator with the remark that the leaders of the great political parties had not yet propounded any scheme, and that purely personal opinion inight lead to misconception. A representative of the Press Association waited upon Mr. Campbell-Bannerman, M.P., on Tuesday, who, while preferring not to define his views with regard to the scheme of Home Rule atttibuted to Mr. Gladstcne, said he agreed with Mr. J. Morley that the difficulties to be encountered should be confronted with union, loyalty, and confidence, adding that he doubted whether any detailed scheme had been formulated by the ex-Premier. Mr. T. D. Sallivan, M.P., weaning at Tuesday's meet- ing of the Irish National League, said there could be no doubt that Mi. Gladstone had applied his mind to the set- tlement and determination of the Home Hole question, and this was a most important and cheering fact for the Irish people. Mr. Gladstone had gone far in advance of bis can- temporaries in the direction of Irish reform, and thev hoped he would. crown his good works in that direction by this glerious,oeasure of self-government for the Irish people. , He dented that there Wee any desire in Ireland to confiscate the land; and as to the fears expressed that the Protes- ants wonld be persecuted, he said that Roman Catholics could not forget that throughout England and her dOlnin. ions they were in a minority, and that retaliatory venge- ance might be wreaked upon them if Irish Proteetants scifered. It was not the business of the Irish leaders to formulate a scheme of Home Rule; the difficulty existed for English statesmen. .

STEAD—NOW tbat the ex- citement of the elections is over, the promoters of various movements haviag for their object the release of Mr. Stead have resolved upon immediate action. For some time past an effective organization bas been at work throughout the country, chiefly by means of established Christian arrencies, obtaining signatures to memorials praying her Majesty at once to interpose the Royal prerogative in fa- vour of the prisoner, whese sentence would in ordinary course expire on the 18th prox. The Salvation Army has already succeeded in obtaining about 200,000 signatures to a demand for the prompt release of Rebecca Jarrett as well as Mr. Stead, upon the ground that "any errors which, in the pursuit of the noble object in view, have been cemmitted have been unintentional and utterly insignificant as corn- pere,l with the good which has been achieved in the passing of the Criminal Law Amendment Act." The petition, pre- sented at the Home Office ott Tuesday. is from It to li miles in length, and weighs about five cwt. Sanguine expectations are Ind &god that Mr. Stead may eat his Christmas dineer with his family; but it is understood that Mr. Stead would - personally prefer to serve the full term. The CHAIRMAN in a few introductory remarks said they had great reason to congratulate themselves an the success of the school's. (Hear, hear.) Last year a Sketching Club was formed, which -he; was glad to say bad begun in a very satisfactory manner. When they considered the position they were in say about two years ago, and the position they were now in he thought they had great cause to be satiefieda (Hear, bear, and epplauee.) Mr. W. BEAMONT, who was received with applause, said be felt indebted to the president and council of the School of Art for the privilege they had conferred upon him in ask- ing him to distribute the prizes to the succeseful students. Alluding to the early hiutory of art he said they found in the best and earliest of boaks that arts were then known. In the fourth chapter of Genesis they read th.t.krial Cain produced musical instruments, and that was a branch of art I which was the girder of the beautiful art which was taught In that school and the successful students of whichthey were to reward that night. He did not know that. anything was said of drawing, but with regard to the early age at which drawing began most singular proof was afforded by portraits, of which there were some in the British Museum I and in the French Museum they were innumerable. Hav- ing alluded to several curious and interesting incidenta in the history of art, Mr. Beamont said that that School of Art was a great benefit and a great credit to the town of War- rington. (Hear, hear.) He believed that the very first germ of that school began with Mr. Pletcher, although be did not meditate such a thing as a School of Art. But he began by setting a good example in pen and iuk drawing, arid thathe (Mr.Beamont) thought Was really the first start, but it was a leng time in growing as everytatng good did take a long time to grow.- It did not spring up all at once to perfection. (Hear, hear.) He congratulated them on the wonderful success attained and wished they would go on and prosper for many years to come. (Hear, hear, and ap- plause.) Mr. Bearnoat then distributed the prizes, after which Mr. Jame RYLANISS proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Beamont for his kindness in cansenting to distribute the prises. He was sure they were all glad to see Mr. Beamont, as he was a good friend of the School of Art. (Hear, hear.) There was another reascn why they were glad to see Mr. Beamont, and that was that they never heard him speak without learning something and hearing something that was interesting. (Hear, hear.) Referring to the work of the scheeta he said that considering the size of the school and the town, he thought they had sent out a larger num- ber of good artists than any other town of a similar size. He need not name them as they all knew them. He thought, however, that every year it was becoming more difficult to attain eminence in art. It was quite clear that the standard was increasing rapidly, and that pictures which 50 years ago would he thought most admirable would now be thought little of. It was increasingly difficult every year for anyone to obtain a livelihood by art. It was, however, not the ob- ject of that *school to make artiste; they had tut to teach the grammar of art, and they hoped that would lead to great benefit. (Applause.) Mr. R. GARMET7 seconded the vote of thanks. It was a pleasure, be said, to see Mr. Beamont at all time., as he seemed to have an almost inexhaustible fund of informa- tion on almost any and every subject. Be did net know anyone in Warrington who could give them so much inter- esting knowledge that that gentleman could. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He wished to give one word of encourage- ment to those who had not been successful. They kaew that a line had to be drawn somewhere, and a large number of those who had not absolutely won might- take credit for having been very near the goal. Ile thoutht the prizes that had been given were very gratifying, and lead been well earned. (Applause.) The vote of thanks was then heartily accorded, and Mr. Beamont having responded, the proceedirgs terminated.

div.p: L

will vote with the Parnellites as they have dune before, in order to overthrow a Liberal , Government. There will then be a deadlock which will be followed by a dissolution, and another appeal to the country. A cheerless prospect certainly, but it shows at least how farseeing the great leader of the Liberal party was when he asked of the nation to return the Liberals to power with such a majority as would make them independent of the opposition of either the Tories or the Parnellites. It is just possible, of coarse, that the leaders of the Irish party may bring themselves to accept such a scheme of Home Rule as Mr. GLADSTONE is at present formu- lating, for, although none ot the pro- jects which are imputed to him are au- thentic, it can hardly be doubted; after what he said in Midlothian that, states- man like, he is preparing for the future. In that case the contingency which Mr. PAR- NELL has in mind would arise; the 86 votes of the Nationalists would be given to the Liberal party, and Mr. GLADSTONE would be I in power with a majority of izo or 130, after allowing for the defection of a score or so of weak-kneed brethren who are sure to fall out of the ranks when the order is given for a "quick match." But we must confess that we have not much hope of so agreeable an issue out of the present complication. , There is reason to fear that the Parnellites will over-rate their power; that they will de- mand more than it will be prudent to give; and in that case a verdict must be sought at the hands of the whole of the electors with the issue distinctly before them. When it comes to that, the Parnellites may find that they hwe stirred a power which will leave them helpless, and which will put back for many ye trs the cause they have at. heart. There is no living Statesman who will go further than Mr. GLADSTONE in conceding all that can be conceded in the ' direction of Home Rule consistent with the maintenance of the integrity of the Empire. There is no living statesmen, as Mr. I'ARNELL admits, so capable as he of framing a wide and at the same time a just measure or Home Rule. Let the Parnellites beware then, when the time comes, that they do not once too often fly in the faze of their best friend. It will be an ill day for England if Mr. GLAD- S ['ONE should leave the Irish problem un- solved ; but it will be worse, a thousand 1 times worse, for Ireland,

THE death of three men at Winsford hop, as it was alleged, "prolonged exposure and refusal to drink spirits," has not unnaturally excited some controversy. Dr. Fox, the Medical Officer of Health who reported on the case, expressed himself as confident that their lives had been shortened by their absti- nence for, being teetotallers, it is stated that they Lank nothing but tea with ginger in it. It transpires that this is not quite correct, the ginger having been put in some hot gruel; and further, that one of the men drank spirits—brandy and hot water; but was no better for it. This, however, is not generally known. Those who take "a nip to keep themselves warm have, therefore, felt themselves specially fortified by this new instance of what they r - gard as the stupidity of teetotallers •, and the case, being a rare one, and backed by medical opinion, has been pressed into service in many places and in many ways. The particulars seer, to have come to the knowledge of the editor o" The British Medical Journal." He briefly stat,.s the facts, and what little he has to say in the way of comment is as follows: —" This is a very extraordinary and eccen- tric statement, which it would be difficult to suggest a phySological explanation." After this the teetotallers may breathe again ; it is an admission on high authority that there are even yet two sides to the question. Dr. Fox is told that his statement is an eccentric one, and that it is not iupported by modern physiology. " Who shall decide when doc- tors disagree?" And the answer, as it seems to us, is that people must exercise their com- mon sense, and decide for themselves. Lord WOLSELEY is not a teetotaller, but he has no faith in spirits for sustaining men in case of ," prolonged exposure." His first great suc- ' cos was his conduct of the Red River Expe- ditrzn, the record of which is for the most part a "Tale of the Dismal Swamp." so trying vas the work of the men in the track- less marst)es of Canada that the regimental medico—me of the Dr. Fox type—pro- nounced his opinion that it could not be satisfactorily ,:arried out upon temperance principles. Bit General (then Colonel) WOLSELEY was a man to have his own way; he stuck to his motto of " Tee- totallism for herd work and prolonged exposure," and the result was a bril- liant triumph fo• temperance. It was the same in the Soud;n ; the long trying march before the memogble battle of Tel-el•Kebir was undertaken at lord WOLSELEY'S orders on 1 a temperance reginen. No spirit was served i 'out; but who shalliay there was any lack of spirit when that gand charge was made which shattered in E moment the power of ARABI PASHA? Urd WOLSELEY is HO fanatic ; but he knows that success is at- tained by adopting he means tgot he end ; and he has found from obseMation and actual experience tha_ the military machine I is more perfect in its tction when it becomes I"a total abstainer.'' There is nothing, of course, new in ths—except to such men as Dr. Fox. The Same tale is told at the North tole as 7.•tne Equator. in the deep mine as I well asan the mountain, and that is that the abstaiier, other things being equal, has a Vecided advantage over the man who " drinks spirits." Dr. Fox's statement is cer- tainly "eccentric ;" and it is not too much to say that his physiology is out of date.

The Government seem to recognise that they must make hay whilst the sun shines, and that it will not shine long—for them. If they kept on as they have begun, and attained an average length of official life, everybody who voted Tori at the last election would be either a magistrate or an earl, or something; in some office or other. But they look for- I ward to having to shuffle off the Government 1 coil suddenly, and are making the best or worst of.it. Hence the additions to the peer- ' age ; hence the jobbery in the way of ap- pointments. Lord SALISBURY, early in his Premiership, broke the spirir if not toe letter ! of the law by making a relative a Charity 1 Commissioner over the heads of men in every way better qualified for the post than his nominee. The, LORD CHANCELLOR recently gave a vAluable appointment to one of his near relatives—a GIFFARD and now Mr. HENRY GRAHAM is made Clerk of Parlia.- ments by the Lord President of the Council. Of Sir ERSKINE MAY, as Clerk of the House of Commons, everybody has heard; he is re- cognised as the highest authority in all mat- ters relating to Parliamentary procedure. But who 13 Mr. HENRY GRAHAM ? Who is he that he should be given the first prize—

1,(3.000 a year with little or nothing to do? ;He is nobody in particular; but he happens to be a son-in-law of Lord CRANBROOK, the President of the Council, and that explains everything. Is it not time, that in some form or other, a stop was put to this sort of thing ? The working-classes have, to their credit, shown a strong feeling against the granting of pensions; but what is this but a mode of pensioning one's ton-in-law? It is galling, at any time, to see that a big sum is paid for very little work ; but there would have been some sense of fitness in the appointment if it had been given, as it ought to have been, to a tried servant of Parliament like Sir EASKINE MAY. But " blood is thicker than water " ; and " blue blood," it seems, does not shame to pauperise cousins and sons-in-law by pro- viding incomes for them at the expense of the public.

THE Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority had a distinguished sitting on Tuesday—dis- tinguished, and at the same time disgraced. It seems that the authorities of Somerset Huse have intimated that, for the future, in• - stead of a sixpenny stamp, as heretofore, two stamps—one of los and another of ss—will be required for agreements passing under the seal of the Authority. As there are numerous contracts, the Clerk suggested that the ixthor- ities of Somerset House should be communica- ted with. This was reasonable enough and innocent enough ; and to ordinary minds no opening was afforded for a display of poli- tical feeling. But it would seem, that the minds of some of the members are not of an ordinary kind. Mr. PARR suggested that they should write to "that good-natured man, JOE CIIAMBER!..AIN, about it." Mr. STOKES said "Mr. .;11AMBERLAIN would put it right directly," whereupon Mr. PARR added—'' He would not buy much that he could steal, wouldn't that fellow." This is a nice imputation to make against the charac- ter of an ex-Cabinet Minister ! It is libellous lin the extreme, and the best answer that Mr. CHAMBERLAIN could snake would be to Isend Mr. PARR a writ. And why " JoE " CHAMBERLAIN? Why not '' JIM" PARR Or JOE" STOKES? Why, indeed, should Mr. I CHAMBERLAIN'S name be dragged in at all?' He is not connected with Somerset House, , and the hardship of higher stamp fees is taking place not during a Liberal but under a Tory Administration. But bad blood will , show itself. It is impossible of course to I make a silk purse out of a certain animal's ear, but Mr. PARR might for all that try to— moderate the rancour of his tongue; Remember When.the judgment 's weak the prejudice is strong. If this is beyond him, and if he will insist upon "evil-speaking. lying, and slander- ing," he should be made to smart for it. '

CHRISTMAS DAY has passed over in this district uneventfully, but that does not mean that there has been a lack of enjoyment. There is a portion of the population whiCh has felt the pinch of trade depression ; but we are right, we believe, in concluding that dis- tress is not extensive. Indeed, if ...at were the case, we are quite sure that a move would have been made for relieving it, for neither the disposition nor the means are wanting among our leading men. Neither Runcorn nor Widnes is in an average condition as to trade, but at the latter place there are signs of improvement. At Warrington some ' five or six hundred (including children) availed themselves for the Free Dinner given yesterday by the Mayor to those who stood , lin need of it. Let us hope that the turn of fortune's wheel will be such that these people will be in a position, next Christmas, to provide a good meal for themselves and I have something to spare. It is well that the poor help each other freely when trouble' , comes, or this would indeed be a hard world Ito live in. SHELLEY speaks with a poet's I tenderness of "the unremembered acts of I kindness and of love "—unremembered, it may be by the authors, but treasured as "happy memories" by those who have felt their influence. And thus it is that life is sweetened and brightened. Let us live and let live, and help one another; in this spirit, we wish our readers "A Prosperous I and Happy New Year."

SERIOUS AFFRAY IN A HOUSE AT RAINHILL. I At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Owen Garritty and James Lyon, young men, were charged with stealing a , gun, worth 30s, the property of John Simpson, labourer, Rainhill. The prisoners were also summoned for assaulting Simpson. Mr. J. W. Knowles defended. , From the evidence for the prosecution, it appeared that I Simpson, who Ls an old man, had for several weeks past j had a young woman named Bridget Kildare, who belonged I to St. Helens, living with him as his wife. On Saturday t night they went together to a grocer's shop at Stoop', I Rainhill, calling on the way back at the Red Lion public- I house Here they had several drinks, and met the prisoners, j who followed them home and into the house. They corn- menced pulling Kildare about. and Simpson took down the gun, which was charged with powder but no Mitt, and threat- , ened if they did not let her go to use it. Lyon wrested the I gun from him, and struck him a blow on the shoulder with the butt and, injuring him 'seriously. He was under the care of a doctor, and had beea unable to work since. The prisoners then ran out of the house with the gar, which was found near the house some days subsequently. In re- ply to Mr. Knowles, Simpson std he should have S' shot the gun off " a Lyon had uot stopped him. Mr. Knowles ar- gued that Lyon acted in selt-defence. Garrity was dis- charged, and Lyon, whe bad previouely served two mouths for an assault of a bad charizter, was fined 20s and costs, 7s 6d, or a mouth.

"PALL MALL GAZETTE" EXTRAS.—OIIe of the two "Extras" of the "Pall Mall Gazette" is a Popular Guide to the House of Commons. It is a complete record of the eleetions which have just taken place, furnishing numbers polled in ISBS compared with those of 1880. There are also valu- able- electoral maps, and portraits of tie more notable members, with briet sketches. It is a wonderful publication at theprice—sixpence. The other "Extra" is a reproduction of a series of sketches by the late Richard Doyle. One set is, as far as it goes, a comic history of England; the other is "The Startling Story of Tommy and the Lion." They are very funny and very clever. SALFORD AND TILE Snit, CANAL.—A special meet- ing of the Salford Town Council was held on Wed- nesday, for the purpose of confirming a resolution passed on the 11th inst. declaring it expedient to promote a bill in the next session of Parliament em- powering the Corporation to invest a quarter of a million sterling in the Manchester Ship Canal. The proceedings were remarkable on account of the strength of the language used by one or two speakers during the course of a heated debate. Those in favour of the proposal became at last ap- prehensive that the resolution would not be carried with-the majority required by the Borough Funds Act; they accordingly moved the adjournment of the debate for a week, which was agreed to, not- withstanding the strong remonstrances of those who are opposed to the money of the ratepayers be- inEspent in the manner proposed. THE REV. CANON CARE AND Coilvocknosi.—The poll in the case of the two proctors to be elected to Convocation by the clergy in the Archdeaconry of Warrington. which was demanded at the meeting of clergy held in St. Luke's Church, Liverpool, last week, closed on Friday. There were four candi- dates for the two positions of proctor—the Revs. Canon Warr, Canon Carr (St. Helens), Canon Penrhyn, and .1. W. Diggle—and at one o'clock, the time for the close of the poll, the Venerable Arch- deacon Bardslev (who presided) said :—lt is now time for us to Close the poll. Out of a possible con- stituency of 98 voters 82 have recorded their votes, and of these 56 have been given in favour of Canon Warr, 49 in favour of Canon Carr, 26 in favour of the Rev. J. W. Diggle, and 19 in favour of Canon Penrhyn. It only remains for me to congratulate Canons Warr and Carr, and to wish them health and strength in the performanceof their duties.—On the motion of Canon Warr, seconded by Canon Carr, a vote of thanks was given to Archdeacon Bardsley, and the proceedings terminated. THE MERSEY TUNNEL. --- ARRANGEMENTS FOR TUE OPENING.—The Princess of Wales, M. Glad- stone, the Duke of Westminster, and the• Earl of Derby will take part in the proceedings connected with the opening of the Mersey Tunnel. The royal party, who will be the guests of the Duke of West- minster at Eaton Hall, will leave Chester on the morning of January 20th by special train, on the Great Western line, for Rock Ferry, where the royal saloon carriage will be attached to a Mersey Railway train, which will convey the distinguished party to Birkenhead. There the Prince and Princess will ascend by the lift to the surface, and will re- ceive an address. Alter inspecting the machinery for the ventilation of the tunnel, the royal party will proceed on foot down the gradient into the tun- nel, which the Prince will thereupon declare open. They will take the train for Liverpool through the tunnel, which will be specially illuminated for the occasion. On reaching Liverpool the Prince will receive 11 deputation, consisting of the Mayor and Corporation of Liverpeol, and the Princess will be presented by Major Isaacs, on behalf of the Mer- sey Railway Company, with a memorial jewel. A luncheon will subsequently be given, probably at the Town Hall, and the royal party will return afterwards to Eaton Hall,, Trains will commence to run through the tunnel, Birkenhead and Liverpool, on the day of opening.
