The Rev. J. Lockwood reported that the total amount,of county rate for the quarter was £1,139 14s 3J, being a decrease of £ll les 2d. A NEW ROAD TO FRODSHAM. Mr. Fisher said the Runcorn Guardians had considered whether it was advisable to provide stone breaking As a test In Runcorn for able bodied persons unable to get work. After nearly half an hour's delibera- tion, the jury returned the following verdict:—" That the deceased came to his death by accidental drowning, and the jury cousider that the stones piled on the quay in so dis- orderly a state by being too close to the edge of the basin rendered accidents highly possible; also that great 'negli• genes has been shown with regard to the lig!iting of the gas lamps along the quay." Mr. Rosenburg said the matter should be reported to the Trust.

The Deputy Coroner said the preservation of life is a eerious consideration, and It seemed that the regulations \ with reference to the lighting of these lamps had not been attended toms they ought to have been. The realities of the deceased were interred in the Run- corn Cemetery on Tuesday afternoon, in the presence of a large concourse of EpectAtwe. Turner being a Lance- Sergeant in the Volunteers, the funeral was ef a military character. The volunteers to the number of 60 rank and file and nine eetgeants, commanded ley Lieut;nsnte Rhodes • and Joule, proceeded to Weston Point, end on erriving at the residence of the deceased, the body was received by the sergeants of thecompaniem, and placed in the hearse. Pre- ceding the hearse was a firing party with rerersed rifles, ander the command of Colour-Sergeant Mort. The band, playing the "Dead March" in "Saul," followed. Near the hearse walked the sergeants, and behind were the ;datives and numerous friends of the deceased. The main body of the volunteers brought up the rear. The route of the pro- cession was through Weetoc, and at the cemetery the Im- pressive service was condaetted by the Rev. T. M. Armen. A beautiful wreath made by Mrs. Stoll, of High•street, was placed on the coffin by the sergeants. At the conclusion three volleys were fired over the grave.

SCARLET FEVER IN RVNCORN.—Four deaths from scarlet fever have occurred in Runcern during the past week. This disease is very prevalent in the tdwn. T. THOMAS'S DAT sr Havrow.--The Halton charities were distributed to the poor of the parish., on Monday, the main dispensed amounting to over £2O. There were present —the Rev. J. Lockwood, vicar who presided ; Messrs. C. L. Evans, agent to Sir Richard Brook, Bert.; Seam Smith, eenior, one of the surviving trustees of the Eaton Charity; Thomas Wright, and Hugh Rowe, overseers; Churchwarden Rutter, and William Nixon. RUNCORN TONTINES.—The Wellington Hotel Tontine has paid 1310 per member, and a dividend of 6s per mem- ber has been declared by the Irwell Mutual Benefit Society, held at the Egerton Arms Hotel. The members ef the An- derton Toatine, held at the Anchor Inn, Brunswick-street, , held their annual supper on Tuesday evening, when shout '5O persons sat down to an excellent repast served t.T the landlady, Mrs Anderton. The dividend paid was las 7d per member. The division of the fends of the Runcorn Foothell Club Tontine has averaged 19.5 per member. PRIZE DISTRIBUTION AT THE NATIONAL SCHOOLS, WIDNES —The children att-nding St. Mary's Parish Church and St. Paul's Church,Suneay Schools were presented with Prizes for good attendance and knowledge of scripture on Monday evening. The Rev. A. P. amid' in Wilson presided over the proceedings. Mr. James Williams read a satisfac- tory report of St. Mary's Sclnfol, and Mr. Thomas Hughes read an equally gratifying one with regard to St. Paul's Schoels. Aire. J. Wright-Williams, wife of the vicar, dis- tributed the prizes. Mrs. Williams and the teachers were thanked for their gervices. ; • RUNCORN LIBERAL ASSOCIATION. A meeting of the I Liberals of the Runcorn polling dibtrict was held on Toes- day evening in Bethesda Lecture Hall, Mr. James Nand- i ley occupied the chair. Mr. Handley was unanimously re- appointed president of the association, with Mr. S. C. Beckett, vice-president. Mr. 0. Leak was re-appoinned secretary. Representatives to the " Liberal 300" of the Northwich Division woe ',elected, and the various ward 1, committees with chairmen and secretaries were appointed. It wee decided to hold monthly meetings open to Liberals i and Conservatives for the discussion of current political ' matters and other subjects. The Rev. Was. \rause will be , asked to read his paper on "Notional Expenditure" at the first meeting to be held a month hence. FRITH BREAKFAST MOVEMENT AT WIDNES.—The CM- Ii mittee'appointed at the meeting held at the officers' room, 'Drill Shed, Widlier, on the 17th test ,to draw 110 a definite scheme to relieve the distress amongst the school going children of poor parents, met on Tnesdey in Messrs. Gasket], Deacon and Co.'s Lodge. There were present Bev. G. Bond (in the chair), Rev. T. Finaeme, Meters. H. Wade, Deacon, Thomas Sadler, and S. B. Stringer. It woe stated that the eases reported by the various teachers had been in- vestigated, end after .a full discussion it -was decided that while there were m ony cases deserving of relief, the dWrees was not such at present as to call for the appointment of a public committee ; bet a list of the deserving cases sub- mitted le to te" sent to each of the various mintstets in the town.

• OFIRISTMASTIDE AT RUNCORN.- Christmas was obeceved naneh in the usual fashion at Ruucorn. On Wedneedap night the tradespeople made theit• show, and the brlghtly gleaming windows and well stocked shops gave the idea that poverty had fled the town. Plenty 17118 on every hand. The establishments of butchers and poultry dealers were. the chief attractions to the hundreds of people who- thronged the streets, and the huge sides of beef, prime pigs, turkeys, and game of all descriptions, all displayed with the greatest profusion WA!) a sight worth the seeing. The displays of the groeers were admirable, and the windows of the drapers were, bright with a wealth of coloured !trader+, Meagre. Uneworth di-playinte many suitable Christmas pre- sents. at beyond all. this outward show there is much poverty inethe town. Many persons, heads of families, ane out of employment, wages are low, /ma altogether the trade of the plane is not in a fi mriah- log &iodide°. It is to be hoped that at this time of feasting and merry making the poor will not be for- gotten by these who hare enough and to spare. On Christmas Eve, notwithstanding a cold atmosphere' I and a drizzling rain, the streets presented a scene of ' animation, " buying in" in being the chief business. About eleven o'clock bands of young men, dressed in singular style, paraded the various thorough- fares, making discordant noises, and acting in a, boisterous but good-humonred fashion. Later the waits went out upon their missions, and their strains of sacred melody were doubtless a source of 'pleasure to those comfortably housed and at ease. IChristmas day was dull and damp, with an atmos- phere of spring-like warmth, and far different from the poetic conceptions of the gladsome festival. The ;railway Ufa° was etteeped, the works were closed, and the teem presented the appearance of Sunday. In the morning services were held in the churches of the establishment. There were good congregations. There were few public celebrations of the day, and the townvpeople had to make themselves merry in their own family circle or with theirfriends. ' Fooeisam. DRUNETCNNESS.—Vdward O'Toole was charged with hay- ing been drunk while in charge of .1 horse Ind cab on Satur- day. Fined 58 costs.--Thonfas Southern, charged with baying been drunk in Berney -street on Saturday night, was fined ss, including costs.--John Jones, charged with haring been drunk and disorderly in Sankey-street on ' Saturday night, was fined 5s and costs.—A young man named Sauce WRS sent to gapl for 14 days for having been drunk and disorderly at Town Hall on Saturday night.— Mary Tawny Was gent to goal for a month for having been drunk and disorderly in Cockhedge-latte on Standay mora- ine-- Patrick Garrity, for being drunk on Sunday morning, was fined ss, including costs.--Martin Lyons, - drunk and disorderly in Butterrnarket-street, on the 13th ' inat.,fined ss, including costs.----Llerby Holahan, drunk and diamderlyift Horeomarket-street, on the 14th met, fined 5a and coats. Dantationiess AND Assert:rt.—John Hoarty, -a young man, was charged -with having been drunk in tetotland-road on Saturday night, and also with having assaulted P.C.s' Bruen and Bell. RUNCORN v. LIVRRPOOL AND DISTEI7Cr.—,-On Saturday afternoon a match was played at Runcorn against a team with the above title, which bad been got together by J. Hampton-Jones, of Liverpool, a very fast and interesting game being played. Direitly after three o'clock Jonas started the ball for the District team, Johnson preventing -the ball getting into his quarter. W Hughes and Lewis moved on a bit towards the District goal, and at centre

Antrobus threw to Speakman, who in 'Curn.gave to Lunt. Gregson and Tickle here were quick In stoppirig the intro- Sion. After some loose play Speakman got the ball and took a splendid though not successful drop at goal, a dead ball resulting. Play followed the drop out in the borne quar- ter, Wilcock, Jones, and Grierson playing a strong forward game. The borne front rank", however, got the ball out of all danger, Lunt receiving the ball from Speakman, the District quarter was reached, Lout being only pushed in touch a few yards froin the goal line. Play merged into the middle of the ground, where from a scrimmage Antrobus gave Speakman the ball, and the latter ran in, after some good dodging, behind the poste, Woods kicking a goal from the place. Starting again from the centre, play became very fast, lodging awhile in the home half, some good ex- changes being made by Johnson and Speakman, which relieved the pressure a little. Cox, Joule., Lewis, and Dunbavand taking on the ball to the centre, H Hughes fol- lowed with a Aronz effort, getting up to the line. Play then located awhile in the District half, where Hugh . .

Hughes smartly threw the ball to Speakman, who dropped a magnificent goal. Nothing further of note took place up to crossing over. After changing ends H Hughes started the hall; no.return was made by the District. Johnson fol- lowed and made a strong effort to make headway, Roberts and Woi dward checking him. The borne forwards, headed by Lewis, Wainwright, and Hughes, were successful in taking on the hell to the District half, from which Gregson kit ked to Woeds ; the latter was collared before be could rid himself of his charge ; scrimmages wero for a short time frequent, the District, men playing up with remarkable vigour, and during this period of fast play Woods, made a mistake which let his opponentrr forward up. The ball crossed the line, where Speakman in dropping on it was pushed over, Rorthwick claiming a try, which, on an ap- peal to the referee, was allowed to him. The same player took the place and miserably failed. Nothing farther of note being scored, the home team won an interesting game, viz., two goals, three minors, to District one try. three minors. For Runcorn, II C Speakman played a grand game. Johnson saved splendidly, playing very well, and being well supported by Lunt. Hoeft:9 and Antrobus played a capital half-back game, tacklirg and passing being fre- quently acknowledged. The forwards played a minierate game, four of the ueual pack being absent, namely: Wright, Hall tnd, Dean, and Barns. For the Dietrict fifteen, Tickle, Lloyd, aed Gregson were the best behind the scrimmage. In the forwards, Wilcock, Hampton-Jones, Speddmg, and Grieraon played a sterling- game. div.p: NOTES BY THE WAY.

The meeting of tne North v. South team at Bradford, which fixture originated eleven years ago, resulted in the total defeat of the North team by two goals, three tries, and two minors to one try and one minor. These teams have met together thirteen times, and out of that number the South have been victorious nine times. They certainly played a biter combined game last Saturday than the North, but when we look at the South team being chosen out of four eluhs only, and the North team composed of men from thirteen different clubs, the victory of the Senth loses a great deal of its significance. Huddersfield paid a visit to Manchester to oppose the club of that name, coNsiderable interest being tsken lii the game, which was a very pleasant one. The Mancunian were one try and a couple of minors to good for them, the visions not scoring a single minor. Broughton met on their own ground and for the first time the Halifax team, a splendidly contested game resulting in favour of Halifax by one goal (dropped), two tries, and four minors, to one goal, one try, and one minor for the Grif- fins Broughton Rangers went as far as Rochdale to play the insects of that town, and after a well-contested game vic- tory rested with the Rangers by one goal and one minor to one try and six minors scored by the Hornets. Though the Rangers won, the Hornets had decidedly the best of the game throughout. The match between Oldham and Warrington, played on the ground of the former, was about the finest ever seen on that eroond. At call of time Warrington was defeated by one try and three minors to one minor. The Oldham for- wards are considered the strongest forwards in Lancashire, but, to the credit of Wartiogton, they were completely over- matched. • ' As was anticipated, Wridnee proved too good for Walton, rubbing it in to the Uwe of one goals three tries, and four minors to nil.

Runcorn tackled a fair team raised by Mr. J. H. Jones, of Liverpool. frctn various clnbs in that district, a very plea- east game being witnessed by a large number of spectators, which resulted in favour of Runcorn by two goals and three minors to one try and three minors for the visitors.

Rubinstein, having written to Mr. Rio bert Gladstone suegesting a coalition between Liberals and Con- eervatives, the latter 'attending to foreign affairs whilst the former dealt with domestic legislation, has received the fol- lowing reply:—" Hawarden Castle, Dec. 2lat. Dear Sir,— I should be glad to aee the Tories taking up the questions of the Irish Gervernroent, and co-operation between the two great English parties. Bet the division of the executive which you propose would be unconstitutional and Impos- sible to work. I fear that, as the Toriea will probably WiiBll their hands of Mr. Parnell now that they have got through the election with the Irish vote, party warfare will be the only method of getting justice for Iteland —Yours faith- fully, HERBERT GLADSTODX."

WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightle meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. Ths chair was taken by the hey. G. F. Roberts, aand.there were also present— Meagre. Derbyshire, Appleton, Brown, Ratcliffe, Blackhuret, John Houghton, Kilshall. Gibson, Grange, Humphries, Belharry. Win. Hougkton ; J. C. Sutton (clerk), and S. Sutton (assistant clerk.) TUe CHRISTMAS DISMAY.

In the minutes of the House Committee it was stated that at a meeting, held on the 11th Deeenaber, at which there were present Messrs. Brown, Greening, Ratcliffe, Appleton, and Jolley, the committee made inquiry from the ntatros relating to the, provisions as ordered on the 4th inet. for Christmas Day, and were setiefied there would be , no weete.—Mr. Bnower moved the confirmation of the ' minutee.—Mr. 13aeciewieusr commented on the quantity of fruit (392 lbs.) that had been ordered for the Christmas dinner of the inmates of the Workhouse, and said that The partieulars of this quantity should be epecified. He moved that this be done. Mr. ilowerobjected to eattsfy any such motives se moved by Mr. Blackhuret, If gentlemen were dissatiefied they ought to move a vote of censure on the committee, and if they thought they could do things better than the committee they ought to clear their con- sciences by attending , the meetings of the House Com- mittee. They should be rtmightforward and declare what it was they wanted to bey, and not fight with revered weeper's. The committee had told them that they were Iperfect y eatiefied everything would be used without any witete, and that he again affirmed on behalf of the com- mittee now —Mr. RATCLIFFE said he at tended that com- mittee himself, and he WAS fully satiefied that the fruit would not be wasted. From whet came before that oommittee he Noe perfectly wailed that whatever was left would be put to good use -Mr. Daserromaecconded Mr.Blackhurst's proposition that a return be made an to bow the 392 los of dried fruit Wee need. He thought it RAS a very weak sh• planation by the committee to state that what was left would be used for seine othei purpose. They did not ex- pect this fruit would be use for any other purpose. The amount of fruit was so excealingly excessive that it quite startled the Board when it was read out. He had made in- quiries and he found that a pound of fruit for each indivi- dual withouteny flour to mike a pudding would be excessive If it was not going to be wasted who need fear a returet Mr. Brown 'aud Mr.- Appleton seemed to think it was be- neath the Beard to watch the expenditure of the workhouse or the Union, but they had a public duty to perform, and they were bound as representatives of the ratepayers to see everything was used for the purpose. for which it was pro- cnred.—Mr. BROWN said if that speech of Mr. Derbyshire meant sny thing it meant censure of the committee. The committee had told theta that the fruit would be legitim• ately and properly used, and he was sure there was not Tato7payer that iy,ould not be satisfied with the way the fruit would be need.—Ms. BalCintretsT objected to Mr. Brown Imputing motives to any member of the Board.—Ohe Camisole thought there was no need to impute motives to each other. It waa a simple matter. The committee had made provision for the entertainment of the inmates of the workhouse on Christmas Day, and some gentlemen thought the quantity of fruit was excessive. He did not see any reason why those gentlemen should not have their minds satisfied without involding a vote of censure on the corn- linows : The object is not that; we have in.- cited Mr. Bleckhurst to come to the committee himself.— Mr. BLASE/UMW (to Mr. Brown): 'You should remember that gentlemen opposed to you are as pure-minded as you are, bet it is an old altering that thosb who' are enspicioue of others have guilty minds themselves„--Mr. Meows: No one says that with truer emphasis than yourself.-The motion ef Mr. Blackhnrst was then put to the meeting and carried. e • eCIOOLIP COMMITTEE. This committee reported that the children at radgate had been reported by the doctor as being in gocd health, with the exception. of a few cases' of chilblain.—On the motion of the CHAIRMAN, the minutes were adopted. POE LAW CONFERINCE. The Chairman and Clerk, who attended the recent Poor Lew Conference on behalf of the Board, gave reports of the proceedings at the Conference.—The CHAIkKAN mentioned that at the Conference there was a general feeling that the constitution of the new County Government Boards should be of an elective character. (Hear, hear.) There was decided feeling against the magistrates or any existing au- thority having any voice as ex-•fficio members. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. BLACEHIMST sera tnat unless the new County Boards were elected they might as well stop as they' were. If they had elected members they would then be able to get at their represeatativee. but on the other hand they had no control over them.—The CHAIRMAN said that Sir Charles Dilke stated that he had no doubt wbatever that the pre- sent magistracy would go in for being elected to the new Boards instead of being ex-officio members.—A few remarks . having been made in commendation of the reports of the Chairman and Clerk, the subject dropped. TENWORTRAM ERIDGE. The subject of Penwortharn Bridge was again brought forward, and a memorial to be sent to the Lancaster Annual general Sessions was brought forward for the sanction of the Board, in which the objections to the Warrington Union being called upon to contribute to the cost of erecting the bridge were set forth. It was also stated that Mr. Joe. Rylande intended to move the following resolutions at the Annual General Sessions, viz. :-1. " That a committee be appointed to coasider the.memorial from the Warrington Guardians and report to the Annual General Seesiens thereon'" 2:1 " That no further proceedings be taken relative to Pen-1 worthana Bridge until the Court shall BO order and deter- mine."—The CLERK added that several other Unions were taking action in the same manner as that Board, and he I mentioned that he had written to a number of connty mag- ietrates on the matter, including Sir R. A.. Cross, Lord Derby, and Lord he inmarleigh,from whom he had received ths following replies :—" Ildfile Office, Whitehall, 5.W.,: December 22, ISB3.—My dear eir.—l took 'the opportunity when I was in London of seeing the clerk of the peace for the county of Lancaster in the matter of Pen- wortham Bridge. I am very much afraid that it will now be difficult to find any remedy. The bill was brought in last year tone House of Lords, and was classed among the oppoeed bills in the House of Come I mons; and as the proper time to have raised the objection to the rating clause would have been while the committee was sitting, I do not see how, now that the bill has becomel an Act, any proceedings can be taken. I understand, how- ever, on inquiry, that under section 18, which was put in by the 110L88 of Lords Committee, the Corporation of Preston will still be liable for the repair of half the bridge, and that some bill is in project, as will be seen from the enclosed memorandion. if this bill be proceeded with it may perhapa be poesible to revive the question of the rating cliuse. Upon this point, of course, you will take the best advice. I do not understand that part of your letter which says that my name was included in the Penveorthim Bridge Committee. I believe that I am on the General Parliamentary Commit- tee of the Comity for all parliamentary work, but so far as I know that is a committee which never meets, and I cer- tainly was not on the committee of tho House ef Commons which eat upon the question. If I can he of any further assistance to von please let rue know. Always faithfully yours, RICHARD ASSTIRTON CROSS.—The Clerk to the Guar- dians, Warrington Union."---" Knowsley, Preseot, Dec. 18, 1885. Sir,—l have the honour to acknowledge your tem r of yestercley, with three enclosures, which I will consider before the sessions of the 31st. I presume by what you Fay that it is intended to bring forward some motion on the eubject —I remain, your obedient servant, DERRIL—The Clerk to the Wertington Union."--" Winmarleigh, Gar- stasg, Dec. 19, 1885. Dear Sir,—l have to acknowledge the receipt ef, and to thank you for, you letter of the 17th, with reprints of the proceedines of the Warrington Board of Guardians on the eueject ef the propoeed new bridge between Preston and Penwortham.—Yours faithfully, WINMAR- LRIGH.—Mr. J. C. Suiton."--On the motion of Mr. 13Lecturensr, seconded by Mr. DARRYSHIRE, it was resolved unanimously that the petition to the General Annual Sessions above referred to should be signed by the Chairman on behalf of the Board. In the Irish Court of Queen's Bench, on Monday, Lord Chief Juatiee lav grntj an application to "attach " for rent certain money which had been banked by Lord Fermoy's tenantry on his Lordship's refusal to accept a re- duced rental. This failure of the latest anti-rent scheme is regarded in iJubi as significant. Anotmors OF SNCOND•CLASS Ferors.--The Great Nor- thern Railway Company are enlarging their experiment in connecVon with the abolition or second-class fares. Some, time ago it was notified that tickets of that class would no longer be issued between certain stations in the Midland Counties, and now a similar regulation is issued regarding traffic between stations in the West Riding of Yorkshire and Doncaster. The tickets will still be granted for main-line stations south of that town.

FATAL BOILER Exer.ostox.—On Tuesday afternoon a boiler in rase on the premises of Messrs. J. and .1. Dvson, fire,,r:ck in (eee, '-,tinnington, near Sheffield exploded. Two men rnpl.ycd on to premises were killed, and three others received very serious injuries. The explosion did great damage to the surrounding property. SHOCKING RAILWAY ACCIDENT —A sad railway aecident occurred et Birmingham on Wednesday morning. A lady returning from Stourbridge to Snow Hill station, attempted to leave the train while it was in motion. She fell under the wheels and bad both her legs cut off. She was taken in a dying condition to the General Hospital. Two TITOCSAND SEPTUAGENAHIANS.—A remarkable sight was presented at Leicester, on Wednesday, when 2,000 per- sons over 70 years of age met to receive a new half-crown each and wine and biscuits from Mr. J. H. Cooper, of Ed- ington Hall, Leicester, and the Framework Knitters Com- pany, London. A large nember were over 80, and one old lady, named Ann King, aged 100 years and 10 months, received the gifts. She appeared very lively and quite in- telligent. Stncenee FROM CLIFTON BRIDGE.—A man of respectable appearance, at present unknown, jumped from the Clifton Suspension Bridge at Bristol, on Tuesday. He fell into the river beneath, and was carried away by t'.,e receding tide. The terrible leap has often been selected as 'a means of Suicide, but on the last cceseion, a few months ago, a yoking woman who sprang from the bridge miraeuously escaped with only a severe shock. SmASIIING A MAN'S Sxue.v.—At Staleybridge, on Satur- day, a young farmer, name William Towle, went to the machine works of Messrs. Taylor and Lang to obtain saw- dust. While the works were stopped for breakfast, he went (hewn into the saw-pit, as he kad been accustomed to, to fill hie bags. While so engaged the engine was re-started, and the lever which works the saw caught his head, and his skull was literally smashed.

Otrruaas tw IRELAND —The house of a farmer, named McKenna, residing near Cloghan, South Tyrone, has been fired into. Th 3 bullet passed through the window and struck the opposite wall, paving in its course close to where McKenna and a friend were sitting before the fire. What makes this outrage all the more significant in the excited state of feeling among Orangemen consequent on the recent Home Rule proposals, is the fact that McKenna is a Nation- alist of most pronounced opinion.

A DVISI TN TBAClEDV.—Gnstavus Duggan, Irishtown, near Dublin, has teen arreeted, charged with murdering Hs wife by shooting her. The neighbours heard a shot and found the wife lying dead on the floor, with the prisoner standing over her. A revolver lay beside her with five chambers loaded, and a cartridge case in the sixth. The prisoner states that, his wife took the revolver from the mantlepiece and rresented it at him in jest, saying she would shoot him, net knowing apparently that it was loaded. div.p: 1 TO THE SICK AND WEARY.

A ST. HELENS ROMANCE ANOTHER ENOCH ARDEN CASE. One of the meet extraordinary cases ever known at St' Helens was investigated at the Town Hall on Monday be- fore Colonel Gamble ands Lieut. Col. W. W. Pilkington. Jeihn Edwards, a farm servant, living at Rainford, was sum- moned to show cause 'why orders should not be made upon him to contribute to the support of the four childret ef a woman named Janet Westhead, with whom he had u, eer. gone the form of marriage. The complainant was repte een-, ted by Mr. J. 0. Swift, and for the defendant Mr. ii• L. Riley appeared. Mr. Swift stated that the four summonses against the tee- indent were of a somewhat peculiar character, and differed touch from the ordinary run of bastardy summonses which came before the Bench. The complainant was married in the year 1859, and up to the year 1871 she lived at Crank. brow with her husband, a Man named John Westhead. In April, 1871, her husband left her without giving her any idea as to where be was going or whether be was going away altogether. But he left her with a baby a month old and a large family in addition. She heard some months afterwards of a man being killed at Maghull, end it was suggested to her that it was her husband. She found that the man had been buried, but she saw some of the clothes, and thought they were the clothes of her husband. How- ever that might be, whether they were Weethrod's or not, Westbead did not appear to have been dead, bat from 1871 up to 1877, and for some little period afterwards she did not see or hear anything of him, and in 1877 she and the defendant Edwards went through the ceremony of marriage at a Liverpool chard). From that time they began to live at Crank-brow, and they lived together comfort- ably under the impression for a lung time that they were lawful man and wife. Mrs. Westbead subsequently had four children by Edwards, but shortly after the second child was torn in 1879, Mrs. West- head was horrified to find that her first husband—her law- • ful husband—turned up at Crank. She never 'spoke to him, but one evening she met him. He did not speak to her, but he had spoken to other aeople at Crank, and stayed there a night or two. He (Mr. Swift) would have no difficulty whatever in proving that in the year 1879 Weethead un- doubtedly was ite the flesh, alive and kicking—(a laugh)— but Westhead did not clatm his marital rights. It was sug- anted to him bra witness that he should claim his lawful wife, but he said she might go and live with Mr. Edwards, and for anything he cared they might live next door to him. He then left Crank, and had not since been heard of. Until the Ist October last, Edwards lived with Mrs. Weathead, arid they lived as husband and wife, and it could not be , seriously contradicted that during their intimacy and co- , habitation there bad been four children born, in respect of ' whom these summonses were Witted. The children had looked upon the defendant and Mrs. Westhead as their law- ful parents, and they bad lived with them at their house. I The defendant had for s. ven years been working for Mr. Richard Pye, farmer, and be bad acid he was willing to give her something towards the maintenance of the children. He said he would do so, but he had not done so, and the complainant asked for enters for reasenahle sums to be made upon him. lie (Mr. Swift) believed that Edwards had regu- larly received £1 per week as wages, which he had el ways handed to Mrs. Westhead. The defendant seemed to have been a very decent husband, or a substitute for a husband, and he (Mr. Swift) suggested orders of 3s Scl or 3e per week in reference to each child. Mrs. Janet Westhead, the complainant, was then called. She gave evidence in support of the statement of Mr. Swift, adding that her enaiden name was Janet Rennie. She was married to John Westhead at Rainford, on the 14th March, 1859, aed produced a copy of her marriage ceitificate. • She lived with him as his wife until April, 1871, when ha left her with seven or eight children. Some months afterwards she went to Magbull and saw some clothes. She married Edwards (0 the 10th January, 1879, and between 1871 and that time she bad not I seen her husband Westhead. She married Edwards at St. Edward's Church, Liverpool. A child Was burn on the 28th May following her marriage, and Edwards, who had pre- viously been in lodgings, teen came and lived with her. He gave her a sovereign before the child was been. Since he began to live with her he had only been away on two nighte. The second child was born on the 10th April. 1879, the third on the 17th August, 1880, and the fourth on August 24th, ' 1883. After the birth of her second child she SAW West. bead once, but they did not speak. She had no doubt at all that it Was Westhead she saw. Edwards was working at West Leigh at the time anti she told him that the had seen Westhead when he came home. He had previously heard that from the neighbours. Edwards asked her if she had aeeken to him and she said "No." She added that he might mete and claim her, but Edwards said he (Westhead) would not have to have her if he (Edwards) could help it. He left her three months ago.—LieutaCulonel Pilkingeon : What has become of the children left by emits' husband ?-1 Cemplainent : Five are alive now—one ma-tried and liring , at Parr—two are in service at Mr. Agnew's, on* is at home, i and one at Southpott.—ln reply to Mr. Riley, Mee. div.p: OUR LONDON LIME it

LONDON, WEDN'ESDA.T. I Alter the excitement attendant upon the General ' Election, a term of peace might have been looked 'for before the hurly burly of Parliament begins.- This is a reasonable expectation that has been woefully disappointed. IS ever since 1868, when there was talk of Irish Church and Land Bills, has the public mind been so profoundly • agitated as durink the past ten days. The announcement that Mr. Gladstone had been drivento admit the neces- . sity of considering Home Rule as within the range' of practical politics was immediately followed by the building up of all kinds of detailed schemes which were more or less plausible according to the individual ability of the 'constructor. The most positive assertions affecting particular statesmen were made, and the political world was in a con- stan't tumult. A pernicious system, borrowed from America, of sending a messenger to a prominent public man, and demanding a statement of his opinions, has been intrOdusedhy the news agencies. With-singular unaniniity the gentlemen addressed have refused to say a word in reply, asking that at least they might have the alleged plan' before teem as a precedent circumstance to giving an opinion upon it. In the American press there is nothing more striking than the frank mannsr in which an intccviewer sets down the details 'of his own dis- comfiture. He graphically describes how he has • • been snubbed, and all but kicked Out. It comes to so much per line, and as he cannot make up his quantity in one way.-he does it in another. The. proceedings Of English public men under this system of torture have been less emphatic. Their withers are as yet unwrung, iind they have been content with politely declining to be drawn,. their statements to this effect being recorded with sus- picions verbosity. Out of all the rumours and inventions and con- ,/ jectures something certainly is known. The main '• point is that which was first simply stated, that Mr: Gladstone, viewing the results of the elections In Ireland, has come to the conclusion that the de- mands of the people must. be seriously, examined, and, ai far as comPatible with jealous care for the integrity of the interests of the empire, conceded. There is no plan drawn up, no confabulations with • Mr-Parnell, and neither agreement nor disagree- -, fluent among the leaders of the Liberal party—this last for the sufficent reason that no opinion has been sought in consultation. Even the manner in' 'which affairs shall be brought to ahead is not de- cided. It rests not with one party, but between the two. The initiative will rest with her Majesty:s Government, who have the first word in Parlia- ment. Upon this also there are also varions rumours current. It is said, inter alio, that immediately on . the meeting of Parliament a vote of confidence will be challenged. This looks like running their head against a stcnetwall, but it is not so mad as it seems. It is adadmirable expedient for forcing the hand of Mr. Gladstone. The attitude safest and • best for him. is to stand aside, a looker-on, prepared to act at a favourable moment. Let the Conserva- tive Government wriggle about in the effort to save themselves End their places. When they have de- monstrated their inability to cope with the circum- Stances 'of the hour, then will be the time Zor Mr. Gladstone to step. forward. But if a vote of con- , fidence he it once proposed he will find himself in- a difficult position. The Liberals cannot vnte con- fidence in Lord Salisbury and Lord Randolph Churchill, in which ease the Government must go, and either Mr. Gladstone will becalled in, or, what • / is more probable, there will -be another General Election.

dissclutiou in the .early spring would be a calamity from which the country has good right to demand to be spared. • We have but just gone through the fire, and trade, already in a bad way, has grievously suffered. But these are considera- tions that will sink into nothingness if they in- • terfere with the aims of party ambition. Lord • Salisbury-, it is certain, has now abandoned his ori- ginal in'eution of attempting to deal 'with the Irish grievance. Mr. Gladstone is a competitor too power- • ful for him to cope with. His game is now to make • . , mends of the mammon of unrighteousness repre- sented by the moderate Liberals.. Having secured a reduction of the Liberal majority by a temporary alliance with the Parnellites, he w,ll no* turn upon his allies, denounce them as traitors to the Empire, and go to the country, appealing to that sentiment of dislike for the Irish people which a generous nation, affronted by sedition in Ireland and uproar at Westminster, is not wholly successful in resist- ing. - This is 'regarded, as a patter of tactics, not only very promising but it is, the sole one open to Lord Salisbury. We may, therefore, confidently as- sume his adoption of it, and be prepared for the disturbance of ,trade consequent upon a general election in spring. - There is very lietle either in the atmosphere or the outwan gaped of London which indicates the near approeli of Christmas. The butchers' shops, it is true, ale beginning to dress themselves fotth, and here an I there hangs on the outward walls a disgustinglr fat "beast " bred and fed by more or less distinguished people whose names are given at full length. There is something rather new than • desirable in connection with this Method of adver- tising. In one of the maia thoroughfares an in- genious butcher has for the last few days congrega- ted three or four overgrown and unhappy cattle, destined to furnish forth some Christmas feast. The poor things lie or stand there all day long, per- haps in their sleep babbling of green fields. Ido not think this ingenious person would obtain my • -custom. It does not appear a desirable preparation , for the dintur table that your beef should have apa.ased a miserable week lying on the pavement saisaid the dirt and turmoil of London town. The weather, as far as it has gone, is altogether against 'the notion of Christmas. The spell of keen wintry ' :weather that mark al last week has disappeared, land nowawe have what is emphatically called, " muggy " weatheniSometimes it rains; always it is dark ale foggy. • ',But the street S" ara crowded anti so are the shops. . roaring trade is being done which will in eome efaint measure go to make up for the bad times con- temporary r.ith the General Election. The fashion- able co-operative stores first amongst which stands toe Army and Navy--are a sight to see. :They gold the population of a small town, and it is almost impossible early in the afternoon either to enter or being in to get out. People seem to have at left ,a 1 their errands for the laat moment, and now -win a rush aro frantically grubbing at all the cornters. It is said, and T believe with respect to sone circles it is true, that the habit of sending out Cariatmas cards has greatly decreased. The fashion of late years haai been, if a Christreas card is sent at all, to have your own particular card, with your own device upon it. But whilst this withdraws many customers from the ordinary common places of the season it has no appreciable effect npon the .aggregate sale. One of the largeat purveyors of Cluastmes cards told me to-day that the sale this • year was greater than ever he had known it. - Of the new Parliament almost exactly one-sixth of the total number are what Mr. Disraeli invari- '----,ably called "gentlemen of the long robe." That barristefs should be attracted to the House of Com- mons is a meter of small 'wonder when we consider ' the nunaher of professional prizes that may there 'be drawn. It must be a matter on-testi-burning to the laborious and more or less successful practi- tioner to find men of no standing at the workinr, bar suddenly promoted over everybody's head mad advanced to the highest seats in the profession. 'Chore is the case of Sir John Gorst fbi example. Sir • Jobnie a very able gentleman, and withal an ex- ,Ceedingly pleasant one. But after 'a pretty long career, in which he has been incited to labour by the necessity of living, he has utterly failed to oh- tain'any position at the bar. Yet when the Con- • servatives by a fluke gain office he is straightway pitchforked into the position of Solicitor General, and has his foot on the ladder which surely lead § to the judicial bench. Sir John h a.s, in fact, been scarcely two months Solicitor General before he is spoken of for the judgeship vacated by the promotion of Mr. Justice Lopes. Lord Randolph Churchill, who hes the great recommendation of faithfulness to friends, is pushing his friend ahead. • But 80 start- ling is the proposition in this case that the Lord - Chancellor himself, a striking. example of promo- tion through party influence, has, it ia said, declined to nominate him. In'this case Mr. Grantham has received the appointment. But Mr. Grantham is a gentleman who makes a bare living at the bar, and has never distingniaed himself; perhaps be- cause he has had so few oppostunities. With these bught'examplea before them it is small wonder that . barristers dock to the He use of Commons, though whether that is desirable•lor the Chamber and for theintifrests it should promote is -quite another thing, . . If the time should r ver come when Mr. Gladstone • -should seek an interaiew with Mr. Parnell in order 'to discuss Home Pule, he will have one qualifica- tion not widely spread amongst Engliahmen. He ,is accustomed correctly to pronounce the name of the Irish chic': Nearly all Englishmen, all as far 418 I have noted, with the exception of Mr. Glad_ stone, call the leader o! the Irish party Mr. Par- .

GAS. Sir,—Tte weather to-day has been anything but sug- gestive of Christmas time, and many would not be sorry when evening came, and the blinds could be drawn and the gas lighted. To be gathered round the fire on Christmas Day, telling seasonable tales mad macking seasonable jokes, is very pleasant; but when the light from the gas is so dismal as it has been to-day in my abode, it throws a kind of wet blanket over the whole affair. It is to be hoped that with the commencement of 1886 the Gat Committee will begin a new era of light, and let us have gas of a little more paver and brilliancy than they at present supply. —Yours, etc., Warrington, Christmas Day, 180.
HOW THE WARRINGTON ELECTION WAS WON.

(MR. JOHN WHITE-6N—iiii Sir,—The Morning Post of Tuesday week contains a letter upon this subject, which is certainly a remarkable produta- Coo. It is quite true that members of the great "unpaid" have at times shown themselves strangely insensible to the requirements of strict justice, but as a rule when a magic,. trate publicly expresses himself one generally looks for as high a standard of truthfulness as is expected from ordinary mortals. One remembers, not without gratitude, that the great Sir Richard Cross once announced with all the solem- nity and gravity which' becomes a man Rho thinks be has made a brilliant discovery, that a "lying spirit" was (and is) prevalent, sad to the Tory party in Warrington I would commend the due consideration of that assertion in reading the effusion of Mr. John White in the paper above referred to.

Mr. White says that the Tory victory in Warrington was not due " te the Irish vote and Parnellite influence," and further, that "II is well known throughout the town and freely admitted by the Liberals themselves that the bulk of the Irish vote was not given to the Conservative party." I have no hesitation in saying that the seemed of these state- ment at any rate is a pure invention. Every Liberal in Warrington who was actively engaged in the last election knows only too well to what an enormous extent the inch Vote was recorded for Sir Gilbert Greenall, and it is well known that this fact is admitted on the Tory aide by the highest authority on the subject. It is all very well for the Tories, who, now as always, despise the Irish people, to try and repudiete their alliance with them, seeing that failure has followed the unholy compact, but there is no getting over the fact that the Tories in Warrington did everything they could to secure the votes at the recent election of the men whose support they are now as anxious to say has not been given to their cause. The placards announcing one of the Tory meetings specially invited "all Irish electors" to attend. The two Irish meetings held in Orford-street, uncle,. s auspices of the association described by Lord Randolpu Churchill as "a legion of foul fiend," were specially graced by the presence of local leaders of the Tory party, a magistrate being amongst the number. Mr. Pamirs "manifesto" was placarded all over the town, at whose expense those who saw the printer's name attached will judge , and in numerous other wave, all that the ingenuity of men could do was done to detach toe Irish vote from the Liberal party and to secure it for the Tories. lam quite pr-oared to admit that these efforts would have been only parti illy successful if they bad not been aided by help from other sources. The Tory party in Warrington owe their success partly to the local lieutenant of Mr. Pernell.—Mr. Felix Loughlin, who, with a bitter hostility to the Liberal party, which, to me, is quite inexplicable, has used hie influence to the utmost in purettading his fellow-countrymen to vote Tory. When Mr. Parnell dietributes his rewards he cer- tainly should not overlook this faithful henchman, who may some dav be grateful for his Resistance. Mr. John White cannot deny also that the Catholic priests rendered great service to the Tory cause. In spite of assurances given by more than one of then to the con- trary, at leaet four Of them did alt that they possibly cou'd to serve the Tory Ctu se. How fee the frequent visits of Sir Gilbert to the clergy hpuses at St. Mare's and St. Alban's,and to the Catholic day schools produced this result ' I cannot pretend. to say, but one thing is certain that at to previous election in Warrington has there beet such har- teeny and cordiality between the Catholic priests (with wee I exception) sodtbe Tory carali4.to who was supported by the I Orangemen of the borough. Future events may tbrJw some light upon the present anomaly. It I. true that, little band of Catholics, undeterred by any and every influence, no matter LOA powerful, remained I loyal to party to whom they owe all their privileges, and to these men all pritisa is dnP; yet the fact remains I that Air Gilbert Greenall has bean el( cted member for War- I riOuton. not by thfl strength of Toryism, but by the votes of the Roman Catholics of VA borough. The Influence of the Faie Trade movement, the improved organization of the Tty party, the assistance of that " slimy " classic orgaa to which the intellect cf local Tory- ism pours itself twits,, a week, and the new club in Sankey- street. have each at:Al all added somewhat to the strength of the Tory party, itiol as a Liberal I would not despise any I element of ermngth in any opponents; but in enite of each and all if the conditions I have enumerated Warrington would not have returned a Tory to Parliament if Mr. Par- nell and certain Catholic priests had not thrown their weight Into the scale against us. A few worda more and I have done. The present Patti,- went cannot last long. Already tha Irish party find ti at I the "bread "which the Tories were to give them as a reward for their support is likely to be but a "Stone." Their disappointment will 104 them to discover that "in- gratitude" to politics,aa.^B as in other *aye, insures its own punishment. Before long, Mr. Parnell will be a sup- pliant at the feet of the 'man whose motto is CO "be just And fear not." Then the country will probably have to decide upon the most momentous question of modern times, viz, "a just and equitable scheme of Horne Rule for Ireland." Mr. Gladstone,is tbeponly living man to whom this great nation may safely entrust so vital a matter, and he certainly is the only English statesman iu whose ability and honesty the Irish people have confidence. Let the Liberals of War- rington therefore take coneage ; every day will improve the eituation ; let every attention be paid to education and organisation. Let our local leaders, one and all, show their determination to abolish the present mierevesentarion of the borough, and depend upon it before very long another opportunity will be afforded mot rescuing Warrington from the clutches of Toryietn.—Yours, A. B.

The bodies of three lnf ants were found on Tuesday in the Metropolis, and are believed to have been murdered. Lord Robert Montage, who some years ago joined the Church of Rome has returned to the Church of England. Professor Geddes has been appointed by the Duke of Richmond Principal of Aberdeen University, in succession to the late Rev. Dr. Pirie, TES CaSTLETOWN ROCHE TRAGPDY. —On Saint. day last the prisoner made a lengthened address to the jury, in the course of whhh he protested his inns- refine. The learned Judge expressed his entire and absolute concurrence in the verdict, and sentenced the prisonee to ' death, fixing the execution for the 20th January. William Sheehan, who awaits execution for murdering his mo her, brother, and slater, has made a confossion of his guilt. He is preparing a nariative of how the tragedy was carried out. He is anxious to have it placed in the Attorney- denerars hands before Tuesday next, when his brother-in- law, David Browne, will be pat upon trial for the same mur- der. Sheehan still protests that Browns is innocent.

OF PRIZES.

1 The annual distribution of prizes to the members of the F and G Companies of the 2nd u.RN. teok place in Run- corn Public RAI/, on Monday evening. There was a large audience, Lieut.-Colonel Ashton conducted the proceed- ings, and he was supported by Captain Hazlehurat, Captain Jo'Me. Lieutenants Timmins, Rhodes, Joule, and Gardiner. I—Celonel Ashton. who was received with applause, said he I deeply regretted that his opening remarks that evening should be words of sorrow and of condolence Most of them, no doubt, had heard of the sad death of Lince-Sergt. Turner, of the Runcorn corps. He had been a member of i the Runcorn corps for something like five or six years, (Int- ; ing.which time he had been punctual in his attendance, I wite winning the respect of every mern'aer of the company. He IVO not only expressing his oan feelings, but he was ; sure the regret ,of the officers, non-commissioned officers, and the members of the Runcorn dettchment, when be said ' how sorry they were at the occurrence, and how sincerely Ithey condoled with his widow, parents, and every member of his family. He bad now to congratulate the Ruecern de- -1 tachment upon the continued progress it had made, not only I in numbers, but in efficiency. They had increased from well to good and good to better. Six or seven years ago the Run- t corn detachment did not number more than 50 or 60 men. i'Last year they had incrested to 170, and he was now pleased to tell them that they attained the maximum !strength of over 200. (Applause.) A good deal of this success was due to the, interest which the officers and non- commissioned officers bad. taken in the drill. He had always felt that unless they took an interest they would not And l the men doing so. The whole battalion had increased dur- ing the past five or six years from 600 to 000 Two more companies had been established, one at Devenhain and ' another at Farodon. That woulil make them eleven com- panies in all, and he hoped that by that time next year , they would have been able to make their battalion 1,200 atrosg. It was his ambition to raise the battalion to that strength, and he looked to Runcorn to help him to do it. (Applause.) Be felt sure, judging from the progress they I had made, that there would be no difficulty in forming three companies in all of 100 each. (Hear, hear.) He ! hoped by that time next year that would be an accom- plished fact. Having referred to the general bearing of ! the men in camp at Southport during the summer, Colonel ' Ashton assured them .that be felt proud of his regiment. i (Applause.) RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD. special meeting of this Board was held in their Board- room, Town Hall, Waterloo-road, on 1 nesday morning. The Rev: Canon Barclay occupied the chair, and 'there were present the Rev. Father Penneßy and Messrs. Pritchard and Lea. P.ESViNATION OF Mu. Batsccm—A letter was read from Mr. P. Briscoe, announcing his resignation through health.—The Cbeirman said he was sure be was only speah- ing the sentiments of every member of the Board in ex- pressing his deep sorrow that Mr. Briscoe bad been com- pelled to rdiltot more particularly for the reason assigned —ill health. He had been a val u.hie member of the Board, always in his place, and taking great interest in the educa- tion of the poor.—Mr. Pritchard remarked that Mr. Briscoe had been a member of the Board for' eleven years--from the Commencement• of the.Board—aad on all occasions he bad with great uplghtness and conscientiousness discharged his duties. On his retirement from public offices they could only express the hope that his recovery to health though slow might be sure and that he might be spared malty years to enjoy private life. FARNWoRTII GRAMMAR SCHOOL. ANNUAL PRIZE DISTRIBUTION. On Tuesday evening the ennuil prize dietribution to suc- cessful minders took place at Farnworth Grernmar achool. The cheir was taken by Major Cross, who was supported on the platform by the Head Master (Mr, Watts), the Rev. (ir. Bond, and M.-sers. F. H. Goseage, E. Carey, and R. Lewis. 'there was a crowded attendance. The listen MASTER announced that the following were the successful echolars :—Upper form: Latin, 1 Knowles, 2 Kyle; mathematics, 1 Knowles, 2 H. S. E.ttock ; English, 1 Knowles, 2 Kyle; French, I Knowles% 2J. R. Bate ; science, 1 Knowles, 2 Kyle. Lower form: Latin, 1 Mercer, 2 Sherratt ; mathematics, 1 C. A. Bate, 2 Sherratt ; Eng- lish, 1 Mercer, 2 C A. Bate arid Sherratt ; science. 1 C. A. Bate' 2 Franklin; drawlua. 1 J. H. Smith, 2 Ward; music, 1 J R. Bate' 2 Mercer. Mr. Watts then gave an account of the method of study for exeminatione which was adopted in the school, and, referring to the fact that Knowles bad taken all the first prizes on the upper form, he said that Knowles was about to leave the school to g 0 to business, and be could only wish him succees in whatever line of life he might take,up. (Applaysa.) The CHAIRMAN then delivered the prizes to the various successful echolars, after which The lines> Memo., resuming his remarks. said that in speaking of the present condition and progress of the school his rematks would not be wholly congratulatory, and aet there was, he waft thankful to say, a very considerable amount of what was encouraging as well as of that which was the reverse. In the first place they had room there for CO boys, but during that terns there had been only 32. On the face of it that appeared as a discouraging fact, but he thought it was not altogether so diecouroging as the hare statement might make it appear. It must be borne in mind that they begun virtually as a new school two years ago, and there practicelly having been me school in' the neighbourhood of a Grammar School character, naturally those boys of Grammar School age would be sent to echeole at a little distance, as he knew they had been sent to War- rington and Liverpool, and they could not expect that buys would be taken forthwith- from those schools and sent to that school. All they could possibly hope to obtain at the outset were those boys of average school are whose perenta anxiously desired that they should have a Grammar School educetior. The Board Schools also took a lot of boys whe would otherwise come to them. He did not wish to say one word egainst the excellent education given at the Board SchOols, and it was a fact that must be borne in mind that the educat'on given at the Board Schools was of such a caeraeter tnsi Ineny nateats Were tilet;sfieel with it albo, if they could not hare got such an excellent educalion at the Board Schools, would—ten years ago, for instance—have sent their children to that Grarniner School. (Hear, hear.) There was also an erroneous notion on the pert of some parents that they :night send their boys to that Grammar School for a year or so to finish off their educetion. That was a mistake, as they could not finish off a boy's education in a year, the character of a Grammar achool education be- ing so essentially different to that which is given at Board Schools. Unlees they got a boy for three years they were not able to give him the full benefit of a Grammar School education. Mr. Watts then mentioned that there had been eight candidates for the two free scholarships of the school, and the two who were successful were J. T. Griffiths, who received 750 marks out of 1,000, and J. W. Clibbern, who received 725 marks. Having given a few particulars as to the 'examinations, Sc., he said, with regard to the distribution of prizes, that some held that it was better not to give prizes, but be thought that so long as the competition for prizes was open and manly, and so long as it stimulated the better feelings and not the worse he thought they could be doing no harm by offering them. (Hear, hear.) 'rhe prizes were undoubtedly an encenragenient to the studious, who received in a public manner some acknowledgment of their hard workaluring the seesion. To those who had not received prizes he must ask them not to be discouraged by that fact, bat to work all the harder and endeavour to emulate these who hart succeeded. (Hear, hear.) In conclusion, Mr. Watts spoke in commen- dation of the services of the astietant master, Mr. Atkinson, and mentioned that the training of the boys for the dramatic performance that would be given that evening was entirely the work of Mr. Atkinson. (Loud applause.) The Cumumater said it gave bins pleasure as the chair. man of the governors to see that room so well filled, hat he must say oa behalf of the governors that they had been 'so badly filled hitherto with students. He hoped that that would be shortly remedied. As regarded what Mr. Watts had jttst said about prizes, let him remind the bop that the great thing in this life was perseverance. They would be sure to get prizes of some kind if they perseveres. (Hear, bear.) It gave him pie mute to see the two who bad been stewed from the elementary schools had shown to well there and shown themselves so competent to take prizes. That ought to be a .strong inducement to the different elementary schools to send their best scholars to that school. (Hear, hear.) It was certainly very creditable to young Knowles, and he (the chairmen) hoped he would succeed in his future career as he had succeeded there. (Applause.) j That school war as much thelea as anyone's, and he, hoped I they would strive with the governors to make it as efficient as possible. If they did so they would find the governors would respond to their Call. (Applause.) Mr. Gosseaa said be could only speak to a certain extent with regret :hat the people of Widnes bad not been able to see the advantages that had beets put before them in that school. There was there one of the oldest foundations in the kingdom, of which be thought the governors had taken a correct view, and personally he could not help regretting, after the governors had done all that could be done for that school in the most liberal manner, that they had not been more strongly supported by the ihhabitants of Whines. Generally speaking, when a thing was taken up in Widnee, earnestly and with a desire that it should be successful, it was supported earnestly. Individually—he did not speak for the rest of the governors—he felt great disappointment at the support that school received from the inhabitants of , Widues. If it was going to be relegated into a school that i would simply be a Board School, nothing could express his disappointment. They had not been supported by the Shop- keepers or by anybody, or nearly everybody, who ought to have put their hands in their poc',,ets. They thought that , the most prosperous people in Widnes—the shop-keepers— ' should support a place where their children could receive an educeticen no' less good than could be received at Eton or Harrow, or any other great public school. There were none of them older foundations than that, and there wee no reason that he could see why that scheol should not compare with Eton or Harrow, Clif- ton or Winchester, and why the scholar educated there should not be of as good standing as those from other public echeole. That was a case, he said, in which the people them• selves ought to put their bands into their pockets to sup- port an Institution like that, mot simply for the name of the school, but to support it as an educational establishment which should tore out scholars as capable as any other school in the United Kingdom. He could only ask that , all thaw: who were there would farther take into considera- tion whetbea that school should be a success or vat ; and whether that grand old institution, with its former remin- iscences et good men tanned out, should be made to support itself, and not be allowed to sink into oblivion. He made I an earnest appeal to them not to let the school go down. There ought to be A feeling among therm who have money in their pockets, at thousands in Widnes bad much more so than the manufacturers, that they Were the people to whom that schoel tiolonged, and that they were the people upon whom the soccesa of the school ought to depend. (Hear, I beer, and applause.) Mr. LEWIS then made a statement as to the position of the IC:1001, At the present moment, he said, the governors wanted, in order to clear the foundation from debt, the surn I of £6OO. He had often himself been struck with the , philosophic manrer in wbich the governors at their meetings I looked open that bad state at affairs. Even at their very last meeting they still took an encouraging view and made a resolution that they would make one more grand effort to wipe off that accumulated debt of £3OO. That £6OO Vac - tinily represented the loss on the working of the school from the day of its opening uo to the present time, and the school at preaent was really working at a 1034 of something like £260 a year. Appeals had been made to the public to give support of some deeeription, but the bulk of the peo- ple of Widnes had certainty not responded to ,the appeal. Hs would throw out as a suggestion to that audience arnonest which were many who could afford to do Wbitt fie respectfully suggested, that was that they would indicate to the governors through him, their secretary, their desire or their willingness, at any rate, to centribute a Small annual suns to help out the income of that school. (Hear, heat.) The school fees were originally .£lO a year, then they were reduced to £B, and lately the 'feed had been further reduced to £6 fie per annum, and that figure was about as low as any school which gave co education such as that school rave could afford to adopt. It that reelection of fees had the effect of filling the school, that was to say brought in 80 scholars, the ecbool might then be worked by' the excellent staff of thoroughly qualified masters at a loss of samething like £lOO. and the governors felt there would be little dlin. culty in raising that sum. He was sure they would agree with him that it would be very much better if the school were entirely self•supporting, and the best way to make it so was that the parents of Widnes should make up their • e

div.head: COLLTERY DISASTER IN SOUTH WALES.
div.p: COLLTERY DISASTER IN SOUTH WALES.

LOSS OF 75 LIVES. Just before three o'clock on Wednesday after- noon, a terrible disaster occurred at the No. .2 Col- liery, Manly, near Pontypridd. The colliery is owned by a number of gentlemen chiefly resident in London, and is under the direct management of Mr. Williams Thomas, of Brynawell, who had only just come up from the pit when the sad occurrence took place. Everything science could invent bad been adopted to ensure thorough ventilation. and on Tuesday evening the workings had been ex- amined by men appointed by the colliers, who re- ported that as far as a supply of fresh air was con- cerned everything was in a satisfactory state. The depression of trade had not affected this pit as it had some parts of the district, and consequently there was the full complement, of men engaged. Near No. 2 Pit is the upcast shaft, up which the men who have escaped are being slowly drawn to the bank.

• Upon hearing the report of an explosion, the pit's mouth was soon besieged mall women and children, and many affecting scenes took place. It was in the No. 2, Rhondda division, of the workings that the explosion took place. Its effects above ground were most disastrous. The guides of the pit were broken, so that communication with lie bottom is impossible. The men from the district towards Aberdare have, it is thought. all escaped, but it is feared that many lives have been lost in the other portion of the working. The damage done to the ipit is very groat, and, owing to the fall, it was not at first possible to reach- the emtombed men. I Out of the 773 persons employed, or to whom lamps were given on Wednesday, 520 work / in No. 2 pit, and a large proportion of these work in this fatal division. Up to the time of telegraphing five had been rescued, with burns, and taken to their homes. With the exception of one case the burns are not considered to be very severe. MARDY. THURSDAY EVENING. The appalling calamity that occurred Yesterday has now been measured. The killed do not near the total that was before estimated, but the list of the dead, now accurately ascertained, is sufficiently ter- rible. It numbers 75, and besides these ten lin wounded, and some of them beyond hope, The air is filled with wail- ing for the dying and the dead ; wives and mothers are wringing their hands end piteously moaning in every other I holm in the village. With most of them the spring of tears' is now dried up, and they present an aspect of stricken sorrow even more pitiful than that of those who have still the relief of weeping. One by one the corpses are being carried home through the hushed street, whilst the villagers look on in blank dismay. The lowerti blinds indicate the destinations of the bearers. Women who are not them- selves bereaved draw tilde breath convulsively as these eorpees pass, and shudder to think of the calamity they have so narrowly escaped. For many hours nearly all these poor creatures were victims ef the most sickening apprehenr mon, aril, if many more than was expected have emerged from the Valley of the Shadow of Death, their hearts are all the more sympathetic for those whose fears have become dreadfully realised. The dead, all except one, have been recovered. In one house there has been accumulating a row of no less than eleven coffins, those of relatives and lodgers with them. In no other is there an array so numerically appalling, but in very many the dead are far from being in the singular num- ber. Everything that human sympathy can sueLtest is being done for the poor and bereaved, but their grief is still beyond the reach of alleviation by human hands. Most of tlis 75 died from the effects of aftcr-datty. and, to judge from their looks, passed a Amy without suffering, for their visages are placid, as if in .cleep; but in many in- stances severe burns and fractured thighs, lee, and heads had previously been suffered, the agony contorting the fea- tures. In some cas;,s the injuries were frightful. On. fine yonng fellow had been absolutely cut in two. The coffining of these remains took place as soon as possible altar their re- covery. The comber who actually died in the pit W. 1874. the other man having died after being brought to the surface. Of the ten wounded, four are-in a critical condition. The ' injured are being treated at their own houses by the medical men attached to the colliery and others edio practise in the nelahbourhood. At the time of the accident there were 773 teen and boys in the colliery. A bent one le ten has there- fore been lost. All the survivors were brought to the surface, before midnight on Wednesdav, and by breakfast time this morning the dead had been recovered, with the solitary exception already mentioned. This last poor fellow lies onder a heap of rubbish that is still considered danger- ous to remove.
During the course of to-day the mine has been inverted by several gentlemen of experience and authority. Sir William Thomas Lewis, one of the Royal Commissioners on

Mine, came early in the morning, and, after carefully es- aliening rue plans and mode of ventilation, descended and I inspected the pit and workings. Next came Sir George Elliot, another Royal Commissioner, who made a similar inspection in company with Mr. Wales, chief Inspector. of Mines in South Wales, and Mr. `Randall, his depi.ty. Mr. Evans, Mr. Kirkhouse, and Mr. William lenkine, engineers of other colliers, went down later, in order, if passible, to discover the cause of the accident. There are more severe evidences of the explosion at the top of the pit than in any part of the workings. The firet terrific roar of tha explosion Rave the impression that the boilers bad burst; but when the officials ran out of their °dices and shads, and cast their eyes on the pit mouth, the saw debris of every kind dying in the air and a great black cloud of dust rising and spreading around, darkening the whole scene. All the pit top and it, gearing were wrecked, and an impression prevailed that every maa and boy in the pit was lost. The rush of dust was found to come from the four-foot seam of the downcast shaft. It was in the down- cast shaft workings that the explosion occurred. One of the officials descended the unease shaft one hundred and twenty yard, to a seam above the four foot seam. He, however, soon returned, saying the men were all right there. Meanwhile messengers were hurrying down the valley for assistance. The reddent engineer, Mr. William Thomas, after seeing to their despatch, went with , several men down the upeast shalt to the level of the four- foot seam. The men who had been engaged about the bottom of this shaft were found all safe. The men in the west and north-west workings were next found in safety. Other relirf gangs were meanwhile spreading through the works rind en uggling to open up passages of escape through the falls. After hour, of heroic search the last man was got out who could be found with life in him, but the dead were left till the morning. The work of relief during the later hours of the night was gallantly undertaken by experienced officials from other collieries, those of the Mardy Colliery having been thoroughly exhausted. Happily for the be- reaved families, the passage of the Emnloyere' Liability Act led in this district to the establishment of what is called the Permanent Fund, subscribed to by both men and mas- ters, and out of this widows get £5 for burial expenses, its a weak as long as they do not marry a second time, and 2s el for each child till it reaches 14 years old. In the case of single men the benefit is a lump sum of .£25. With reference to the weather prevailing on Wednesday, it is evident that a low barometer had no connection with the explosion, the distribution of atmospheric pressure he- I ing uraeticelly the same as on the morning of December I 10th, 1880, when 101 lives were Itst at Penygrail. The other great disaster of the year, at Clifton liall,Tendle- bury, took place when the barometer was at its maximum. Up to Tuesday last, the loss of life in explosions reached about 245, the average of the previous 34 years. FRIDAY NIGHT. The Central News says no further deaths are reported. Numbers of friends and relatives of the deceased are arriv- ing from various parts. The injured are doing fairly well, though it it is feared that some cannot long survive their terrible injuries. Preparations are being made for the inter- ment of 20 bodies in the village; but the greater number will be buried at Aberdare, about four miles distant. It is ' honed the irquest will commence early enough to allow of the burial of the dead to-day (Saturday). A local inspector has to-day visited the mine, and a Government inspection.. will probably take piece. _

_ The damage done to the mine is not sl great as might be supposed. Competent persons state that Work might be resumed on Monday or Tuesday. . The improved plan on whicli the mine was constructed has prevented further loss 81 life. The widows and orphans of deceased are partially provided for t)y funds of provideot societies, but it is stated that £lO,OOO is required in addition. Thirty widows and ollfldren are dopriyed of husbands or fathers.
